title: [ROCm][test]Reuse device meshes across ComposabilityTest cases
body:
ComposabilityTest is a MultiProcContinuousTest, so its 8 worker processes are reused for every test in the class. Each test built a new DeviceMesh, and each mesh creates new NCCL communicators. On RCCL every communicator keeps a ~40 MB proxy-ops segment per rank in /dev/shm until the workers exit, so the class accumulated ~10 GB and hit ENOSPC on 10 GiB /dev/shm containers. The failure surfaced as a rank-0 process join timeout.

Build each distinct mesh once per worker and share it across tests. On 8x MI300X with a 10 GiB /dev/shm, peak usage drops from ENOSPC to ~2.5 GB and all 26 tests pass.

title: [FSDP] Stabilize fully_shard overlap timing test
body:
The overlap test emulates compute and communication with fixed-cycle GPU sleeps. DVFS and device contention can change their wall-clock duration between separate single-shot measurements, causing false failures under load.

Interleave reference and test measurements and compare their least-perturbed samples. This only improves timing stability; it does not relax assertions or tolerances, change emulated sleep durations, or add conditional retries or skips.

title: [ROCm][test] Reuse process groups across FSDP hybrid-shard subtests
body:
TestFSDPHybridShard is a continuous test, so its 8 worker processes are reused for every test in the class. test_fsdp_hybrid_shard_basic_setup built a new device mesh in each subtest and test_fsdp_hybrid_shard_parity built new HSDP process groups in each subtest.

On RCCL every communicator keeps a ~40 MB proxy-ops segment per rank in /dev/shm until the workers exit. basic_setup left ~7 GB behind and parity then hit ENOSPC on a 10 GiB /dev/shm, passing only on retry with fresh workers.

Build the mesh and the HSDP groups once per test and share them across subtests. Peak /dev/shm for the class on 8x MI300X at this commit drops from 11.4 GB to 7.5 GB, and all tests pass on a 10 GiB /dev/shm.

title: [inductor] Dump Python stacks on CI test subprocess timeout
body:
Flaky CUDA Inductor tests occasionally hang past 30 minutes and trigger the CI outer timeout. The existing termination path (SIGINT then SIGKILL) yields no diagnostics because processes blocked in native CUDA/Triton code don't act on SIGINT — by the time SIGKILL fires, in-process state is gone.

This PR adds an opt-in SIGUSR1 stack-dump path so test/run_test.py's timeout handler can capture Python stacks from the test subprocess and its Inductor compile workers before the kill sequence runs.

Changes:

1. torch/testing/_internal/common_utils.py
  - install_fault_handler() — enables faulthandler and registers SIGUSR1 to dump every thread's Python stack to the real fd 2 (sys.__stderr__, bypassing pytest's capture proxy). Sets a module-level _fault_handler_installed flag.
  - _dump_subprocess_stacks(pid) — sends SIGUSR1 to pid and all descendants via psutil.Process(pid).children(recursive=True), then sleeps 3s for handler runs / stderr flush. No-ops unless _fault_handler_installed is set, so non-test consumers of wait_for_process don't acquire a SIGUSR1 side effect.
  - wait_for_process — on subprocess.TimeoutExpired, calls _dump_subprocess_stacks(p.pid) before the existing SIGINT/SIGKILL sequence.
2. test/conftest.py
  - pytest_configure calls install_fault_handler() so every pytest subprocess arms the SIGUSR1 handler.
3. torch/_inductor/compile_worker/utils.py
  - _async_compile_initializer installs the same faulthandler/SIGUSR1 registration locally. The default SubprocPool sidecar is started via subprocess.Popen (fresh Python), so the parent's handler does not inherit. SIGUSR1 is otherwise unused in PyTorch.

Result: when the outer timeout fires, the CI log captures Python thread stacks from the test process and every Inductor compile worker, making it possible to identify what's blocking without extending the CI budget.

title: [Inductor] Enable decompose_k by default on ROCm
body:
## Summary

`triton.num_decompose_k_splits` now defaults to 10 on ROCm, the same as CUDA. The HIP special case that forced 0 splits, and the test-only `_DECOMPOSE_K_PATCH_ROCM` override that papered over it, are removed. The tests follow the default.

On MI350X (gfx950, 256 CUs, ROCm 7.2.2) a 474-matmul sweep with `max_autotune` and backends `ATEN,TRITON` does **not** support this as a performance default:

- Of 154 eligible shapes at cap 10, autotune picked decompose K 31 times, ATen 107 times, and the plain Triton `mm` template 16 times.
- Median decompose-K candidate was 22% slower than ATen. When both the Triton `mm` template and decompose K were timed, Triton `mm` won all 18 times.
- The large-K shapes this path is aimed at still pick ATen. 64×128×200000 and 64×64×177147 are 7–20% slower with decompose K.
- Offering the candidate costs about 1.1 s of compile time (p90 1.6 s). A 1024³ matmul, which is not eligible, shows no extra cost.
- Raising the cap from 10 to 20 added a new split on 2 shapes, and neither was more than 10% faster. gfx950 has no single best `k_split`; the winner is spread across 2–256 and differs for fp16 and bf16. Numerics matched eager on 112/154 eligible cap-10 results.

Draft until we decide the occasional small-tile win is worth the compile cost.

title: [AOTAutograd] Fix flat_outs indexing for returned inputs when graph has mutated inputs
body:
Fixes #198609

### Cause
Inside `create_functionalized_fn` in `graph_capture_wrappers.py`, when handling outputs that return inputs directly (`info.output_type == OutputType.is_input`), `flat_outs` assignment used `flat_outs[i]` instead of offsetting `i` by `meta.num_mutated_inp_runtime_indices`. As a result, user outputs overwrote the mutated input output slots at `flat_outs[0...]`.

### Fix
Offset `i` by `meta.num_mutated_inp_runtime_indices` (`out_idx = i + meta.num_mutated_inp_runtime_indices`). Added regression test in `test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py`.

Thanks to @alepot55 for identifying the indexing issue in #198609.

title: [ROCm] Revert Free rocFFT plans (#197425)
body:
This restores the `#if !defined(USE_ROCM)` guard around `cufftDestroy` in `~CuFFTHandle()`, which #197425 (`ffc54724`) removed. On ROCm, destroying cached plans while static objects are torn down at process exit writes into memory that rocFFT has already freed, and corrupts the heap.


## Root cause

The plan cache is a namespace-scope static in `libtorch_hip.so` ([`SpectralOps.cpp:89`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ffc54724e283412d8d396faaee20e281bb7cd67b/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/SpectralOps.cpp#L89)):

```cpp
static std::vector<std::unique_ptr<CuFFTParamsLRUCache>> plan_caches;
```

It is constructed when `libtorch_hip.so` loads, during `import torch`, so its destructor is registered with `__cxa_atexit` early and runs late at exit. Since #197425, destroying it calls `hipfftDestroy` on every plan still in the cache.

rocFFT tracks device memory in a singleton that is a function-local static ([rocm-libraries `gpubuf.h:43-47`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/c283a2bf239eef5d1fe06ddc4b9402634ce99c5c/projects/rocfft/shared/gpubuf.h#L43-L47)), added in [rocm-libraries `184a43da`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/commit/184a43daa41c):

```cpp
static device_memory_accountant& singleton()
{
    static device_memory_accountant instance;
    return instance;
}
```

A function-local static is constructed, and registers its destructor, the first time the function runs. That is the first FFT plan creation, well after `libtorch_hip.so` loaded. Exit handlers run in reverse order of registration, so the accountant is destroyed before `plan_caches`. hipFFT's own `rocfft_initializer` static, which calls `rocfft_cleanup()` from its destructor ([`hipfft.cpp:429-441`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/c283a2bf239eef5d1fe06ddc4b9402634ce99c5c/projects/hipfft/library/src/amd_detail/hipfft.cpp#L429-L441)), is created at the same point and is also gone first. The recorded exit-handler order for a process with 4 cached plans was:

| Exit handler | Destroys |
|---|---|
| #8-28 | rocFFT and hipFFT statics created at first use, including `device_memory_accountant` |
| about #5091 | `plan_caches`, which calls `hipfftDestroy` for each cached plan |

Destroying a plan frees its device buffers. `gpubuf_t::free()` reports every free to the accountant with no check that it still exists ([`gpubuf.h:278-287`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/c283a2bf239eef5d1fe06ddc4b9402634ce99c5c/projects/rocfft/shared/gpubuf.h#L278-L287)):

```cpp
(void)hipFree(buf);
device_memory_accountant::singleton().release_used_bytes(bsize, device);
```

`release_used_bytes` indexes the accountant's per-device vector and writes the new count ([`gpubuf.h:66-77`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/c283a2bf239eef5d1fe06ddc4b9402634ce99c5c/projects/rocfft/shared/gpubuf.h#L66-L77)):

```cpp
if(dev_id < 0 || static_cast<size_t>(dev_id) >= num_devices())
    throw std::invalid_argument(...);
auto& dev_account = mem_account_on_device[dev_id];
dev_account.used_bytes -= std::min(dev_account.used_bytes, allocation_size);
```

The accountant's destructor already returned the vector's storage to malloc, but left `begin` and `end` in the dead object. `num_devices()` still returns the old size, so the bounds check passes, and the `-=` writes into freed heap memory. The full call chain is `~CuFFTHandle` → `hipfftDestroy` → `rocfft_plan_destroy` → `~ExecPlan` → `~TreeNode` → `gpubuf_t::free` → `release_used_bytes`.

A hardware watchpoint on the accountant's freed buffer during the exit of a real `test_ops_gradients` shard recorded 106 `hipfftDestroy` calls making 479 writes to the freed address. If malloc has not reused that memory, the writes land in unused space and the process exits cleanly. If it has, they overwrite a live object or malloc's free-list pointers. A later allocation during exit then fails glibc's checks (`corrupted double-linked list (not small)`, `malloc(): largebin double linked list corrupted (nextsize)`, `malloc.c:4196 (_int_malloc): assertion failed: chunk_main_arena (fwd)`), or the process segfaults. Whether the memory was reused depends on heap layout, so the crash is intermittent.

#197425 relied on rocFFT fixes that make its `Repo` singleton safe after destruction, such as [rocFFT `c2ed8163`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocFFT/commit/c2ed8163725e83f82da37832b4661b2a4bd789f3). The accountant was added later with the same lifetime pattern and no such protection. cuFFT does not have this singleton, so CUDA keeps freeing plans at exit.

## Impact

Since #197425 landed, about 3% of MI350 `default` CI jobs crash at exit after all tests pass, and each crash makes `run_test.py` rerun the whole shard twice. That cost at least 58 hours of MI350 and MI300 runner time between 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-24, and the crash was misreported under at least 10 test names that never failed.

Example jobs:

| Completed (UTC) | Commit | Job | Test file, shard | Crash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-18 05:19:33 | `ffc54724` | [mi350 default 5/8](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35298263879/job/105458835865) | `test_ops` 4/6 | `Fatal glibc error: malloc.c:4196 (_int_malloc): assertion failed: chunk_main_arena (fwd)`, -6 |
| 2026-09-18 06:38:48 | `efa9a072` | [mi350 inductor 2/2](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35300348190/job/105465848463) | `inductor/test_torchinductor` 2/3 | `corrupted double-linked list (not small)`, -6 |
| 2026-09-18 08:04:53 | `d6e690c5` | [mi350 default 8/8](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35309838137/job/105493598322) | `test_ops` 2/7 | `corrupted double-linked list (not small)`, -6 |

title: [Dynamo] Fix getattr on builtin types raising AttributeError when attribute is missing
body:
Fixes #198197

Description

In TorchDynamo, accessing a missing attribute on builtin types/functions via getattr(builtin_type, missing_attr) or inside try...except getattr(...) fell through to construct a fallback GetAttrVariable(self, name, py_type=None, ...).

Because Dynamo treated this as an unmodeled or deferred attribute access rather than raising an observed exception, control flow checking attribute existence (try: getattr(...) except AttributeError:) bypassed the except block and took the wrong branch under torch.compile.

Solution
In BaseBuiltinVariable.tp_getattro_impl, check hasattr(fn, name). If not present, call raise_observed_exception(AttributeError, tx) and return None early.
In BuiltinVariable.tp_getattro_impl:
Return None early under self.fn is object when getattr raises AttributeError.
Check hasattr(self.fn, name). If not present, call raise_observed_exception(AttributeError, tx) and return None early instead of falling through to GetAttrVariable.
Add regression test test_builtin_type_getattr_missing_attr_issue_198197 to test/dynamo/test_tp_getattro.py exercising int, str, list, dict, type, object, float, bool, tuple, and set.

title: [Test] Enable test/profiler/test_trace_validator.py on XPU
body:
Part of #142029.

`test/profiler/test_trace_validator.py` was classified device-specific as a whole. `TestTraceValidatorE2EAgnosticDevice` is already backend-neutral but never generated an XPU class (`allow_xpu=True` was missing), and its one test was held by a blanket skip inherited from a CUDA-side Kineto clock-skew problem that the rule it exercises never touches.

Six commits, reviewable in order; each carries its own test plan.

1. Rename `TestTraceValidatorE2EAgnostic` -> `...AgnosticDevice` (rule B1; no marker files or `cls_name` strings reference the old name).
2. Build the payload lazily in the test instead of `setUpClass`, so a `device` parameter no longer forces a ResNet50 profile at import time.
3. Fix the `privateuse1` -> `ProfilerActivity` lookup (`"privateuse1".upper()` never matches the mixed-case `PrivateUse1` enum member).
4. Classify all three classes for `--hw-classification` (GENERIC / ACCELERATOR / CUDA).
5. Generate the agnostic class for CUDA and XPU (`only_for=("cuda", "xpu"), allow_xpu=True`).
6. Drop the class-level skip and hold CUDA with `@skipCUDAIf(True, ...)`, so XPU actually runs.

### Coverage delta

Intel Arc B580. The XPU and no-accelerator rows are measured on this host; the CUDA row is derived from the framework code, not run.

| host | collected | executing | change |
| ---- | --------- | --------- | ------ |
| XPU (measured) | 24 -> 25 | 14 -> 15 | adds `TestTraceValidatorE2EAgnosticDeviceXPU::test_backward_seq_id_uniqueness_xpu` |
| CUDA (derived) | 25 -> 25 | 14 -> 14 | rename only; skipped before and after |
| no accelerator (measured) | 24 -> 24 | 14 -> 14 | none |

```
$ python test/profiler/test_trace_validator.py
Ran 25 tests in 5.690s
OK (skipped=10)
```

Nothing is removed on any host. Wall clock for the enabled test goes 0.007s -> 5.7s because it now really profiles a ResNet50 training step; the validator indexes 543 of the trace's 1026 backward events, and that count is asserted non-empty so a pass cannot be vacuous.

CUDA is not verified locally (no CUDA host). `skipCUDAIf` keeps the test skipped there, but dropping the class-level skip means `setUpClass`, `setUp`/`tearDown` and the CUDA memory-leak check now run around a test that skips inside its body, where `unittest` previously bypassed them entirely. CI needs to confirm that stays a skip and not an error.

CPU is deliberately not enabled here. `instantiate_device_type_tests` generates the CPU class first, and Kineto latches its `cpuOnly` flag on the first profile in a process and never re-registers it (`kineto_shim.cpp:305`), so a generated CPU class would zero device activity for every later class in the file - measured as 2617 `kernel` events dropping to 0. Enabling CPU needs a `setUpModule` prime and is a follow-up.

title: [dynamo] Wrap observed exception arguments
body:
## Summary

`raise_observed_exception()` may receive `args` forwarded directly from a real Python exception via `exc.args`. These arguments are not necessarily strings or `VariableTracker`s.

For example, `UnicodeEncodeError.args` contains integer values for the start and end offsets. Previously, `raise_observed_exception()` converted only string arguments through `SourcelessBuilder`, allowing raw integers to reach `ExceptionVariable`. This caused Dynamo to fail while formatting the observed exception with:

```text
AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'debug_repr'
```

Convert all observed exception arguments through `SourcelessBuilder.create()`. `SourcelessBuilder` already preserves existing `VariableTracker`s and wraps supported Python values appropriately.

A focused regression test covers an observed `UnicodeEncodeError` containing non-string arguments.

Related to #195901 (`test_builtin.py::TestType::test_type_doc`).

After this change, `TestType.test_type_doc` progresses past the reported `debug_repr` crash and reaches the separately tracked unsupported class-level `setattr()` path at `A.__doc__ = doc`. Therefore, the CPython expected-failure marker for the full test remains in place.

title: [inductor] Preserve repeated tensor aliases in Triton HOPs
body:
The functional Triton HOP cloned every mutated argument independently. When multiple kernel arguments referenced the same tensor, the kernel received distinct storage, so writes through one pointer were not visible through the other and compiled results silently differed from eager execution.

Record the exact input-identity groups when the functional HOP is formed and clone once per group. Carry this partition through proxy tracing, fake tensor execution, functionalization, and reinplacing, since later graph rewrites can merge originally distinct arguments and make current object identity insufficient to reconstruct the original semantics. This covers repeated references to one tensor object, but not distinct views that share storage.

Preserve identity when wrapping functionalized outputs, and keep older or symbolic FX graphs compatible by deriving omitted alias groups only when concrete inputs are available. Functional-only alias metadata is removed before lowering to the mutation HOP.

Add coverage for repeated aliases, mutation through aliased outputs, no-op rewrites that merge distinct arguments, and pass-level cases where an alias group can be reinplaced or must stay cloned because its value remains live or another reinplaced argument shares storage. Also cover symbolic FX tracing, serialization, and legacy graphs without alias metadata.

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/196657

title: [AArch64] Use native GEMV for single-column BF16 GEMMs
body:
Requires `is_arm_neoverse()` to recognize Neoverse V3: https://github.com/pytorch/cpuinfo/pull/435

On Arm Neoverse systems built with the oneDNN ACL backend, decline BF16 CPUBlas GEMMs when `n == 1` and `alpha == 1` so the existing native GEMV fallback is used. `n == 1` makes the operation a matrix-vector product, and these shapes are common during single-token transformer decode.
In official Linux AArch64 wheels, the fallback is OpenBLAS `sbgemm_` when available. Otherwise, CPUBlas uses ATen `gemm_stub`.
`is_arm_neoverse()` is required because this fallback only benefits Arm.

Tested on Neoverse V3 - c8g.16xlarge and Neoverse V2 - c9g.16xlarge.
GCC 13.3 and oneDNN 3.12.0

Workload: GPT-2 BF16 single token decode on one pinned thread

| CPU | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Graviton 5 | 56.0842 ms | 10.5462 ms | **5.32x** |
| Graviton 4 | 75.9550 ms | 14.1522 ms | **5.37x** |

Across other thread counts:
| CPU | Threads | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Graviton 5 | 8 | 11.2110 ms | 4.0912 ms | **2.74x** |
| Graviton 5 | 16 | 8.2988 ms | 4.5431 ms | **1.83x** |
| Graviton 5 | 32 | 7.0627 ms | 4.2545 ms | **1.66x** |
| Graviton 5 | 64 | 6.1616 ms | 4.2753 ms | **1.44x** |

Correctness:
CPUBlas results were compared against the existing oneDNN results across every transpose layout, `beta=0` and `beta=1`, and both aligned and non-aligned dimensions.

title: [dynamo] Constant-fold str and bytes maketrans
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. `str.maketrans("abc", "xyz")` builds a translation table that depends only on its arguments, so Dynamo can compute it once while tracing. Under `torch.compile` normal mode gave the right result, but `fullgraph=True` failed with `Unsupported`, so this is a graph break; a `ValueError` for arguments of different lengths also could not reach its `except`. Adding it to the table of methods that are computed while tracing is safe because the same input always gives the same table. A function whose result changes on every call, like reading the clock, must not go in that table: the wrong result would be baked in. With this PR both cases match eager under `fullgraph=True`.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (`str.maketrans` and `bytes.maketrans`).
>
> `_BUILTIN_CONSTANT_FOLDABLE_METHODS` in `builtin.py` lists builtin methods that `BuiltinVariable` may evaluate at trace time when all arguments are constants. `str.maketrans` and `bytes.maketrans` were missing, so they graph-broke. Both are pure functions of their arguments, so they are added to the table; the existing constant conversion and observed-exception path then handles their results (a `dict` for `str`, a 256-byte `bytes` table for `bytes`) and their errors. A method-specific handler would duplicate that path without adding needed behavior. The error messages are the same in Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14.
>
> **Tests** (under `fullgraph=True`, each fails without the fix)
>
> - `test_misc.py::test_builtin_maketrans_constant_fold`: `str.maketrans` with a dict and with three strings, and `bytes.maketrans`, match eager.
> - `test_misc.py::test_builtin_maketrans_errors` (`str`, `bytes`): unequal-length arguments raise the same error as eager.
>
> CPython tests under Dynamo: `test_str` `StrTest.test_maketrans_translate` and `test_bytes` `BytesTest.test_maketrans` go from error to passing and no test goes from passing to failing in either file; the two expected-failure markers are removed. The other tests in `test/dynamo/test_misc.py` show the same results with and without the change.

title: [dynamo] Fold literal boolean expressions passed to eval
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. Dynamo computes `eval()` of a constant string while tracing, but only if every piece of the expression is on an allowlist. `eval("2 + 3")` already worked, but `eval("1, 2 + 3")` and `eval("1 or (1 / 0)")` failed under `fullgraph=True` with `Unsupported` because the tuple and `or` were not on the list, so these were graph breaks. This PR adds only those pieces. Names and function calls must stay off the list: names can change, so the wrong result would be baked in. With this PR these expressions match eager under `fullgraph=True`.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (fold literal Boolean expressions passed to `eval`).
>
> `BuiltinVariable.call_eval` evaluates constant strings at trace time: first with `ast.literal_eval`, then, when that fails, with a guarded evaluator whose AST allowlist (`_constant_eval_numeric_expr`) admits only numeric constants and arithmetic. Tuple and boolean-operation nodes were missing, so an expression like `1, 2 + 3` or `0 and 1, 2 or 3` graph-broke. This adds `ast.Tuple` (with its `ast.Load` context) and `ast.BoolOp`/`ast.And`/`ast.Or`. Names, calls and non-numeric constants remain excluded, and the evaluator still runs with empty `__builtins__`, so short-circuiting and errors behave as in CPython. A separate evaluator would duplicate the guarded path without improving its semantics. Results are the same in Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14.
>
> **Tests**
>
> - `test_misc.py::test_builtin_eval_literal_bool_expr`: under `fullgraph=True`, `eval("1, 0 or 1")`, `eval("0 and 1, 2 or 3")`, `eval("1 or (1 / 0)")` and `eval("0 and (1 / 0)")` match eager, including short-circuiting past `1 / 0`. Fails without the fix.
>

title: [dynamo] Raise TypeError for empty functools.partial

Under `torch.compile` normal mode caught it too, but `fullgraph=True` failed with `Unsupported`, so this is a graph break; I saw the same pattern in `hasattr` on a plain `object()`. title: [dynamo] Apply __index__ to constant str and bytes subscripts

title: [ROCm] Always eagerly allocate hipBLAS(Lt) workspaces
body:
## Summary

- Make per-operation BLAS workspaces the default on ROCm, as they are on CUDA since #194311. ATen's hipBLAS and hipBLASLt operations allocate their workspace from the HIP caching allocator for each operation, so during capture it comes from the graph's memory pool. `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1` keeps the previous persistent workspace cache.
- Run ATen's rocBLAS operations on internal per-thread handles that release the arena rocBLAS allocates when it creates a handle. Binding a workspace makes rocBLAS free that arena, and the free is illegal under stream capture.
- Give each (thread, stream) its own public handle, the one `torch.cuda.current_blas_handle()` and `at::cuda::getCurrentCUDABlasHandle()` return. ATen never binds a workspace to it, so it keeps its rocBLAS arena, and a workspace a caller binds stays bound. `capture_begin` keeps one spare, so the first request on a capture stream does not create a handle during capture.
- Route TunableOp's rocBLAS GEMMs and solution listing through the internal handle and its per-operation workspace, and give its hipBLASLt GEMMs the per-operation hipBLASLt workspace.
- Enable the existing eager-workspace tests on ROCm, add a C++ handle-pool test and ROCm graph-capture tests, isolate the FSDP2 MemTracker tests from BLAS workspaces, and document the ROCm behaviour in the HIP notes.

## Motivation

A persistently cached workspace is shared by every graph captured on the same handle and stream, so replaying one graph can overwrite a workspace another graph still uses. A per-operation workspace allocated during capture comes from that graph's pool, so no two graphs share one. `test_graph_capture_cublas_workspace_separate_graphs` catches this: with `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1` it faults on SM90 and gfx90a and corrupts its canary on gfx950 (MI355X) and gfx942 (MI308X), and it passes with per-operation workspaces.

## Why ROCm needs a public handle per stream

cuBLAS resets a handle to its default workspace pool on every `cublasSetStream`, and that pool is guarded against concurrent use ([cuBLAS documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html#cublassetworkspace)). rocBLAS has neither: a handle's arena is one buffer, and `rocblas_set_stream` keeps whatever workspace is bound and does not wait for the old stream. A public handle shared by a thread's streams could therefore run GEMMs on two streams in the same arena at once, so on ROCm each stream gets its own.

## Behaviour for callers of the public handle on ROCm

- `torch.cuda.current_blas_handle()` returns a different handle on each stream. A caller that keeps a handle and moves it to another stream with `rocblas_set_stream` must synchronize the old stream first, as rocBLAS requires.
- A workspace bound with `rocblas_set_workspace` stays bound, even after the buffer is freed and after the thread exits and the handle passes to another thread. Unbind it with `rocblas_set_workspace(handle, nullptr, 0)` before freeing the buffer. The handle then has no workspace of its own: its GEMMs use kernels that need none, and other calls make rocBLAS allocate one, which capture does not allow.
- `HIPBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:0:0` makes rocBLAS GEMMs use kernels that need no workspace, but other rocBLAS calls such as `torch.dot` then allocate their own, so they cannot be captured.

The first rocBLAS use on a thread cannot be captured, in cached or eager mode, and this PR does not change that. On MI308X, capturing `torch.dot` on a new thread whose earlier GEMMs all went to hipBLASLt fails at the merge base and with this PR alike. Handle initialization and TunableOp tuning must happen before capture. This is tracked by [ROCm/rocm-libraries#11838](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/issues/11838).

## Cost

- Each public handle keeps the arena rocBLAS allocates when it creates the handle, outside the caching allocator. On MI355X a new public handle took 162 MiB outside the caching allocator, 128 MiB of it the arena. The arena size depends on the GPU and the rocBLAS version.
- There is one public handle per (thread, stream) that requests it, plus one spare once a capture has begun on a device where a public handle was requested. Handles are never destroyed, and an exited thread's handles pass to other threads and streams, so this memory stays allocated for the life of the process.
- ATen's own rocBLAS operations use the internal handles, which hold no arena, so a process that never requests the public handle pays none of this. Two ATen paths still request it and so create a public handle on each stream they run on: MAGMA queue creation and the batched BLAS3 LU kernel.
- Per-operation workspaces cost a caching-allocator allocation per operation; see Performance.

## Validation

MI355X (gfx950) and MI308X (gfx942), same results on both:

- `hip_cublas_handle_pool_test`: 6 pass and 1 skips; with `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`, 2 pass and the eager-only tests skip.
- `test/test_cuda.py -k cublas -k workspace -k blas_handle`: 22 tests pass, 3 skip. With `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`, `test_cublaslt_workspace_eager_resize_and_zero` and both shapes of `test_graph_capture_cublas_workspace_separate_graphs` fail, as expected; the separate-graphs test fails in each of three runs and passes in each of three runs without it.
- `test_graph_capture_tunableop_cublas_workspace` passes and replays a rocBLAS solution; it skips when TunableOp picks none.
- A TunableOp GEMM on a new stream no longer creates a public handle: 0 MiB outside the caching allocator, down from 162 MiB (MI355X).
- On MI355X, the 43 `test/test_linalg.py` TunableOp tests, each in its own process, give the same results at the merge base and with this PR.
- FSDP2 MemTracker tests pass with per-operation workspaces and with `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`.
- Bounded workspace OOM tests raise a normal `OutOfMemoryError` and recover, for rocBLAS (128 MiB workspace) and hipBLASLt (80 MiB), in both modes.

## Performance

Following #194311: BF16 `torch.mm`, synchronized `torch.utils.benchmark.Timer.blocked_autorange(min_run_time=2.0)`, shapes labelled `(M,N,K)`, and one process per (mode, backend) because the caching mode latches into a function-local static on first use.

Two adjustments were needed for the numbers to be stable on these parts.

First, the dominant noise term is a per-process offset, not within-process jitter: the spread of per-process medians reached 4.3 us while the within-process Timer IQR is 0.01-0.8 us. So the run uses **20 alternating-order trials** and reports a **paired** statistic - `eager - cached` within a single trial - with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval and the per-trial sign count. Raising `min_run_time` does not help, since it only shrinks the term that was already small.

Second, that offset was tracked to CPU socket placement. The `gfx950` host is dual-socket with the GPU on one socket's PCIe root; at 11-17 us these GEMMs are dispatch-bound, so the measurement is dominated by host-side launch traffic, and a process scheduled onto the far socket pays an interconnect hop on every launch. Five pinned processes per socket measured +0.6 us for the far socket, and pinning collapsed the per-process spread from 1.95 us to 0.39 us. Both arms are therefore pinned to the GPU-local CPU list. The `gfx942` numbers are unpinned but do not need this: their same-mode control is 0.023 us median / 0.156 us worst case.

The control referred to above is a same-mode null - splitting one mode's own trials in half and differencing them, where the true answer is zero by construction, so the result is the noise floor of the instrument. Two further checks on the protocol: a negative delta is not physically possible here, since eager performs strictly more allocator work than cached, so any negative row indicates drift rather than a speedup; and the eager path was confirmed active in each binary by measuring per-operation workspace scratch after a warmup GEMM, 76-80 MiB in eager mode against 0 in cached mode.

- **Short, launch-bound** (11-19 us; the 64^3 and 256^3 shapes) - eager costs +0.13 to +0.33 us, three of four significant, worst relative case +2.93%.

### Interpretation

The eager cost is CPU-side caching-allocator bookkeeping, and `torch.mm` is asynchronous. On a long GEMM that work overlaps GPU execution of the preceding operation and is free; on a short one, dispatch is the critical path and it shows up in full. The two parts agree on this: every gfx950 shape is launch-bound and all eight carry the cost at +0.16 us, while on gfx942 only the launch-bound rows carry it, at +0.13 to +0.33 us, and the GPU-bound rows are pinned at zero with intervals that exclude +0.3 us. So the data is consistent with a fixed per-operation cost of roughly 0.15-0.35 us, worth at most a few percent on operations short enough that launch overhead already dominates, and absent on any GEMM doing substantial work.

That is the same order as CUDA PR #194311 (0.07-0.85 us / 0.5-5.1%), and below it in absolute terms, despite the hipBLASLt workspace being 76-80 MiB against cuBLASLt's 1 MiB - the caching allocator returns the same block on every call, so workspace size does not enter the per-operation cost.

title: [inductor] Always in-place user defined Triton kernels
body:
This pull request improves the re-inplacement pass by additionally allowing it to re-inplace ops against views of graph inputs. It matches the inverse write back pattern created during functionalization and recorded in the fx metadata. It should always be possible to inplace these functional wrapper ops created this way without tracing back from the epilogue copy, we just have to update the users of the pattern, and we can separately investigate the epilogue copy's eligibility for removal.

I found the original missed re-inplacement opportunity in particular against a private implementation of a model that has integrates custom Triton kernels that writes back to slices, which prevented re-inplacement because the view replay nodes (`slice_scatter`, canonicalized to `_generalized_scatter`) appeared between it and the epilogue copy.

It is inspired by the reply by Claude in #190548 which mentioned that I should probably look at what happens with that PR and an unknown op write to the result of an inplaced op. That PR would abort re-inplacement in this case; this redesign looks at ancestry to associate the chain with its epilogue copy that reflects the changes back to the graph input.

I have used AI-assisted tools to generate the tests for this PR, to create scenarios and tests and get an understanding of how the pass works. However, the changes to the pass itself are my own.

title: [dynamo] Acquire the pairwise iterator when called
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. In plain Python, `itertools.pairwise(0)` raises `TypeError` right at the call. Under `torch.compile`, the same call inside `try/except TypeError` returned as if nothing was wrong, which is a silent wrong result; I saw the same pattern with a zero `range` step. The cause is `yield`: because of it, the body of Dynamo's `pairwise` never runs when it is only called. With this PR the `TypeError` is raised at the call as in eager.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (acquire the `pairwise` iterator when called).
>
> The `itertools.pairwise` polyfill was a generator function, so its body, including the `iter()` call on the input, ran only when the result was consumed. CPython's `itertools.pairwise` acquires the input iterator at call time. The polyfill now calls `iter()` in an outer function and returns an inner generator for the pairs, so pairs are still produced lazily and a non-iterable raises `TypeError` at the call. Keeping a single generator function would leave the timing mismatch intact.

With `keep_inference_input_mutations`, when a user output is an input whose mutation stays in the graph, `create_functionalized_fn` returns the input itself for it, writing `flat_outs[i]` with `i` the output's index in `meta.output_info`. But the traced function returns the `num_mutated_inp_runtime_indices` inputs mutated outside the graph first (`fn_input_mutations_to_outputs` / `fn_prepped_for_autograd`; the same split the runtime wrapper applies to the forward's outputs), so the write replaced one of those and the epilogue copied the wrong tensor into that input. This offsets the index.

Test plan: the new `test_input_mutation_is_output_after_mutated_inputs` fails without the change and passes with it (on 2.14 and the 21 Sep nightly, with the change applied at runtime). test_aotdispatch.py, test/dynamo/test_aot_autograd.py and Inductor's CpuTests are otherwise unchanged with it on 2.14; no existing test reaches this line with a nonzero offset.

title: [XPU] make the device-wide wait in syncStreamsOnDevice opt-in
body:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191900/ made syncStreamsOnDevice() delegate to device_synchronization(), i.e. a device-wide ext_oneapi_wait_and_throw(), instead of draining the SYCL queues PyTorch owns. Those are two different contracts:
1. syncStreamsOnDevice - the work WE submitted on this device has finished
2. device_synchronize - all work by ANYONE on this device has finished

Every caller of syncStreamsOnDevice needs only the narrow one. The caching allocator calls it to make a block safe to reuse, and torch.xpu.synchronize() has always meant it on this backend. Routing them through the stronger wait makes them block on GPU work PyTorch neither owns nor tracks - on the allocator hot path, that means another library's kernels. This file's own comment states the narrow property: the legacy path "only drains queues we own; SYCL queues outside our pools are unaffected."

To be explicit, because the two arguments are easy to fuse: that is a SEMANTIC objection, not the explanation for the slowdown below. I measured whether the device-wide wait is blocking on foreign work here and it is not - after draining our own pool queues it finds only ~11us of anything left, and everything this process dispatches already runs on our streams (Triton included, via
torch.xpu.current_stream().sycl_queue). The contract mismatch matters for workloads that DO share the device with another SYCL component; it does not explain the numbers.

On ARC B580 (BMG/Xe2) this measurably regressed dynamo inference. Restoring the narrow wait is faster in five independent experiments.

Three of them run ONE binary and pick the path at runtime with the environment variable introduced below: one group of runs with it unset (narrow wait), one with it set to 1 (device-wide), the two groups alternating in blocks so that machine drift affects both equally. Nothing else differs between the groups - identical object code in the same install - so build nondeterminism, inlining and install state cannot contribute:
- one binary, env var unset vs =1, on nightly-20260805: faster by 4.86%
- one binary, env var unset vs =1, on current man: faster by 7.43%
- one binary, env var unset vs =1, repeated on main: faster by 8.37% The other two compile the tree twice from a single commit - once as-is, once with #191900 reverted - and compare the two binaries:
- two builds of nightly-20260805, revert vs as-is: faster by 7.42%
- two buidls of current main, revert vs as-is: faster by 4.51%

Measured on BlenderbotSmallForCausalLM, bs=2, --backend=inductor -n10 --cold-start-latency --float32, cold caches, 10-15 measured runs per group.

No mechanism is claimed, and the obvious one is ruled out: measured standalone, the device-wide primitive is CHEAPER than walking the 96 pool queues (~22us vs ~46us in an eager-like regime) and is O(1) in queue count where the walk is O(N). 13 hypotheses were tested and none held, including GPU clock and kernel-execution effects (device-side time is identical, 46 vs 45.9ms for identical work), roreign-queue work (there is none in this process), allocator behaviour (all 110 memory_states counters byte-identical between the two configurations), and cost displaced onto later kernel launches. The effect reproduces robustly; its cause is still open.

This PR keeps device_synchronize() and the fast path intact but makes taking it opt-in via TORCH_XPU_SYNC_STREAMS_DEVICE_WIDE=1, restoring the previous default. The flag is named for syncStreamsOnDevice.

On the planned deprecation: PR #182630 said syncStreamsOnDevice would be deprecated "when oneapi upgrade to 2026.1", and the TODOs here say to drop the latency fallback once a suitable driver is widely deployed. If these callers are rerouted to device_synchronize(0 they inherit a stronger contract they don't need. Separately,
syncl_ext_oneapi_device_wait is an *EXPERIMENTAL* extension whose specification states that shipping software products should not rely on it; deleting the fallback would make it the only synchronization path in PyTorch-XPU

Fixes: https://github.com/intel/torch-xpu-ops/issues/5150

title: Fix Normal.log_prob overflow for extreme scales
body:
Fixes #198579

`Normal.log_prob` currently squares `scale` and `value - loc` before dividing, so intermediate overflow or underflow can produce NaN or lose the standardized residual term for otherwise representable results.

This changes the calculation to standardize first and then square the residual, avoiding those intermediate scale/residual squares. Regression tests cover float32 and float64 maximum and minimum normal scales, plus a large float32 standardized residual.

- TestDistributionsCPU.test_normal_cpu: passed

- compileall and git diff --check passed

title: [DCP] Optimize FsspecReader with Batched cat_ranges and Async Prefetching
body:
## Problem
When loading distributed checkpoints (e.g., FSDP or Model Parallel) from object storage backends (like gcsfs or s3fs), the current `FsspecReader` processes byte intervals individually in a strictly sequential, single-threaded loop. This exposes several performance bottlenecks:
1. **Request Serialization**: Issuing thousands of individual HTTP range requests creates massive connection and latency overhead.
2. **Synchronous Starvation**: Because network I/O, `torch.load` unpickling, and tensor slicing occur sequentially on the main thread, the network stream is routinely starved while waiting for CPU deserialization.

## Solution
This PR introduces a concurrent, double-buffered pipeline and native batch range reading for `FsspecReader`:
- **Batched cat_ranges**:
  - Replaces per-item single range reads with a single `fs.cat_ranges(paths, starts, ends)` call per batch.
  - Range coalescing policy is left entirely to the storage backend. `FsspecReader` passes only paths, starts and ends, so backends that coalesce may do so under their own policy, and backends that do not are unaffected. No capability probing or argument-level fallback is required.
- **Double-Buffered Async Prefetching**:
  - Decouples network I/O from CPU deserialization: a dedicated single-threaded prefetch executor fetches batch k+1 while a multi-worker CPU thread pool deserializes batch k in parallel.
- **Configurable Batching & Concurrency**:
  - Exposes `max_batch_size` (default 64) to bound transient memory and `cpu_workers` to maximize deserialization throughput.

## Benchmark Results

Timings measure `FsspecReader.read_data`.

**Setup:** 8 ranks on a single VM (c4-highmem-96, no GPU is needed for this benchmark); a 44.88 GiB checkpoint on GCS standard bucket

| Strategy | Baseline | This PR | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FSDP (sharded) | 520.56 s | 17.69 s | **29.43x (-96.6%)** |
| Model Parallel (sharded, TP=4, DP=2) | 563.85 s | 34.92 s | **16.15x (-93.8%)** |

title: [Sigmoid] Stabilize AOTI inplace weight identity (#197430)
body:
Summary:

Resolve AOTI constants by exact or unique wrapper-normalized FQN for compatibility with existing snapshots whose generated _run_on_acc/_run_on_gpu wrapper changed.

The `_run_on_acc_<n>` and `_run_on_gpu_<n>` components are generated by lowering partitioning, so wrappers may be added, removed, or renumbered when graph partitioning or ordering changes between otherwise compatible snapshot publishes. In the observed `1140807405/4 -> /17` transition, the cold-loaded AOTI delegate retained `merge.submod_0._run_on_acc_0...ln.weight`, while the replacement archive exposed the same tensor as `merge.submod_0...ln.weight`. The prior exact lookup therefore raised `<wrapper-qualified FQN> not found in Weights` and aborted the update before snapshot 17 became ready.

Also index each packed parameter, buffer, and tensor constant by its namespaced archive storage key. AOTI delegates retain that compatible-snapshot identity from the source snapshot and prefer it during inplace updates, so lowering-wrapper renames do not control weight matching. Storage-key ambiguity is derived directly from the multimap, and canonical ambiguity is derived directly from the current weight set, eliminating separately maintained ambiguity state.

Every update logs an exhaustive resolution breakdown: storage key, exact FQN, canonical FQN fallback, and optional constants retained. Constant metadata is read for both cold-loaded and cached-weight executors, so buffers, tensor constants, and empty parameters retain AOTI optional-update semantics in the child process while missing required parameters still fail.

This is runtime-only and requires no model input or publishing-config change.

title: [dynamo] Match CPython errors for bound __contains__ calls
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. When `__contains__` is called directly with the wrong arguments, for example `{}.__contains__()`, compiled code raised the right exception type, `TypeError`, but with a different message: `expected 1 argument, got 0` instead of `dict.__contains__() takes exactly one argument (0 given)`. The message does not say which method failed, so it shows the error but points the reader in the wrong direction. This is hard to hit in everyday code. With this PR the messages match eager.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (match CPython errors for bound `__contains__` calls).
>
> The `sq_contains` slot wrapper (`_wrap_objobjproc`) raised generic `TypeError`s for a bound `__contains__` call with the wrong arguments: `expected 1 argument, got N` and `this method takes no keyword arguments`. CPython names the type and method, e.g. `dict.__contains__() takes exactly one argument (0 given)` and `dict.__contains__() takes no keyword arguments`. The wrapper now formats both messages with the bound type's name and `__contains__`. Keeping the change in this slot wrapper leaves the other wrappers and method calls unchanged.
>
> Scope: only the message text changes; the exception type was already correct. The `in` operator always passes exactly one argument, so this only shows up when `__contains__` is called explicitly with bad arguments. The same wrapper serves `set.__contains__`, which was also checked manually (`set.__contains__() takes exactly one argument (0 given)`).
>
> **Tests**

title: [dynamo] Preserve hasattr keyword errors and answer exact-object checks
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. This PR fixes two separate problems in `hasattr()`. First, on a plain `object()` instance, `hasattr(o, "foo")` and `hasattr(o, "__dict__")` gave the right answer under normal `torch.compile`, but `fullgraph=True` failed with `Unsupported`. Normal compile giving the right result while fullgraph fails is a graph break. Second, `hasattr(x=2)` raised `TypeError` with an empty message instead of `hasattr() takes no keyword arguments`, which is a wrong error message. With this PR both match eager.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (preserve `hasattr()` keyword-argument errors; answer `hasattr` for exact `object` instances).
>
> - `HasAttrBuiltinVariable` combined the keyword check with the arity check and raised a message-less `TypeError`. The keyword check is now separate and raises CPython's `hasattr() takes no keyword arguments`; the arity path is unchanged.
> - `ObjectVariable` used the generic `hasattr` path for exact `object()` instances, which graph-broke ("Unsupported hasattr call") on absent attributes. An exact `object()` has no `__dict__` and cannot gain attributes, so `call_obj_hasattr` now answers from the represented value when `type(value) is object` and leaves every other value on the generic path. Changing the general attribute protocol would widen the scope without helping this case.

> **Tests**

> - `test_tp_getattro.py::test_hasattr_keyword_error`: under `fullgraph=True`, `hasattr(x=2)` raises `TypeError` with CPython's message. Fails without the fix.
> - `test_tp_getattro.py::test_hasattr_exact_object`: under `fullgraph=True`, `hasattr` on an `object()` for `foo`, `__call__`, `__dict__`, `__class__` and `__str__` matches eager. Fails without the fix.

title: Enable NCCLSymmetricMemory (RCCL) symmetric-memory support on ROCm
body:
## Summary

This PR enables `NCCLSymmetricMemory` on ROCm. ROCm cannot reuse the CUDA path: HIP graph capture, RCCL window registration, and the device reduce APIs do not behave the same way. The changes below are the smallest set that make allocation, rendezvous, capture, and the three device ops work on the tested RCCL stack.

Almost all of the C++ under `torch/csrc` is `USE_ROCM`-guarded. Five fixes are not, and do change CUDA behavior; they are enumerated under "Changes that affect the default path". `NCCL_HAS_SYMMEM_DEVICE_SUPPORT` on CUDA stays at NCCL 2.28.0.

## Problem

`NCCLSymmetricMemory` was CUDA-only. Opening the same gates on ROCm is not enough:

- RCCL `ncclMemAlloc` without CUMEM falls back to `hipMalloc`. Capture rejects that.
- A synchronous `hipMemset` or `hipMemcpy` during Global capture returns HIP 906 and kills the capture (901).
- An async memset recorded on the capturing stream becomes a graph node and can wipe a peer signal pad on every replay.
- RCCL 2.30.4 window registration fails during capture. 2.30.7 succeeds.
- A fused multi-destination reduce-scatter launch faults with `HSA_STATUS_ERROR_MEMORY_APERTURE_VIOLATION` on gfx942 and gfx950.
- A retained handle after process-group destroy launched a barrier kernel through a dead communicator and hit `HSA_STATUS_ERROR_MEMORY_FAULT`.

## Solution

On ROCm, a per-device `NCCLDevCommManager` snapshots RCCL device-API support at communicator init. That snapshot requires CUMEM and WIN to have been set before the communicator was created. Fresh windows use CUMEM plus an async zero on a non-captured setup stream wherever that path is supported. Peer tables upload on the same stream, under a Relaxed capture-mode guard, so rendezvous returns with initialized device pointers. Device comms are created once and cached. Reduce-scatter still launches one kernel per destination. On ROCm, `ProcessGroupNCCL` retires its registry identity before RCCL abort or destroy, and every ROCm accessor that can touch a communicator checks that registration is still live.

The suite runs on any ROCm with RCCL >= 2.30.4 and a host-compatible `nccl_device.h`. MI350 additionally requires ROCm 10.1, because the symmetric-memory defect that motivates a version floor only reproduced there.

## Design choices

**`nccl_device.h` presence is not enough.** A host C++ TU cannot compile every RCCL that ships the header. CMake probes the installed header. ROCm also requires RCCL >= 2.30.4 (`NCCL_HAS_SYMMEM_SUPPORT`), written as `#if !defined(USE_ROCM) || defined(NCCL_HAS_SYMMEM_SUPPORT)` so CUDA's `NCCL_HAS_SYMMEM_DEVICE_SUPPORT` threshold stays at NCCL 2.28.0. hipcc needs CUDA's extended-lambda macro and a local `__half operator+` because PyTorch defines `__HIP_NO_HALF_OPERATORS__`.

**Device API support is a runtime snapshot, not a compile-time gate.** RCCL reports `deviceApiSupport=0` unless both `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE` and `NCCL_WIN_ENABLE` are set before communicator init. A qualifying header can still sit on a communicator that has no device API. `NCCLDevCommManager` records `ncclCommQueryProperties` at register time and binds it to that communicator identity. Turning the env vars on later does not enable an already-created comm. Rendezvous therefore rejects that case outside capture, which is the test that reaches `comm_has_device_api_support()`.

**Capability, not capture state, selects the allocation path.** The CUMEM + setup-stream path is correct outside capture too, so keying on `capture_allocation_supported()` gives one path on a supported stack. HIP only reports capture state for the current stream, so this PR adds no `is_graph_capture_active()` call site: the CUMEM path runs under the Relaxed guard, performs no capture-illegal host wait, and writes the pad and peer tables as immutable host-side setup rather than graph nodes, so a Global capture on another thread does not need a process-wide query. The current-stream `TORCH_CHECK` exists only as the diagnostic for configurations that do not support that path.

**`TORCH_NCCL_SYMM_MEM_DISABLE_CAPTURE_ALLOC=1` keeps the plain path.** It is read inside `capture_allocation_supported()`, so it selects `ncclMemAlloc` plus synchronous memset for allocation *and* a synchronous `cudaMemcpy` for the rendezvous peer-table upload. That is the allocate-then-capture fallback for stacks that cannot allocate under capture, and it is how the two allocation paths were compared: both arms produce the same peer digest, which is what justifies keying on capability rather than on capture state.

**One shared setup stream is created when a qualifying comm registers.** Signal-pad zero and peer-table H2D need a stream that is not the capturing stream. HIP allows `hipStreamCreate` during Global capture; the pre-create is so every alloc/rendezvous reuses one per-device stream rather than creating one per call. Use of that stream is serialized. It is created at registration regardless of the kill switch.

**A host-side wait is illegal under Global capture, even on a non-captured stream.** Moving the H2D copy off the capturing stream is not enough. `cudaStreamSynchronize` on the setup stream still returns HIP 900. `alloc()` therefore wraps its whole `ncclMemAlloc` / async-zero / synchronize sequence in `CUDAStreamCaptureModeGuard{Relaxed}`, and rendezvous does the same for the peer-table upload. The peer tables and signal pad are immutable for the object's lifetime, so they are initialized on the setup stream and are not recorded as graph nodes. `hipStreamWaitEvent` would also work, but it would only guarantee the tables are ready before later device work, not when rendezvous returns on the host.

**Fresh capture allocation requires RCCL >= 2.30.7.** Direct window registration during Global capture succeeds on 2.30.7 (mode stays Global, capture stays active). 2.30.4 fails in worker-side synchronization. Older RCCL still works if the tensor is allocated and rendezvoused before capture.

**`ncclDevCommCreate` is a direct call, then cached per op.** First create during Global capture succeeds on 2.30.7, keeps Global mode and an active capture, and the captured graph replays. All-to-all and reduce-scatter each create a devcomm once and cache it under their own op key, so neither pays creation cost per launch. There is no extra ROCm-only capture guard around create. The symmetric-memory barrier uses the signal pads directly and needs no devcomm.

**RCCL leaks Relaxed mode on window deregister and device-comm destroy.** Direct `ncclCommWindowDeregister` and `ncclDevCommDestroy` change the caller's capture thread mode from Global to Relaxed. Destroy during an active capture also invalidates the capture. Both calls sit in a balanced `CUDAStreamCaptureModeGuard{Relaxed}` so the caller gets its mode back. Same idiom as the setup-stream wait.

**The manager destructor keeps `cudaDeviceSynchronize`.** HIP returns 900 for that wait under an active capture in both Global and Relaxed thread mode, so a Relaxed guard would not make teardown capture-safe. This enablement does not change destructor synchronization.

**Reduce-scatter is serialized per destination, not fused.** The fused launch faults on gfx942 and gfx950 with RCCL 2.30.7. Row tiles that write one destination are safe. ROCm drives the existing shared kernel with a one-slot `ReduceScatterOffsetsInfo` rather than getting a kernel of its own. With `n_owned == 1` the barrier index collapses to `blockIdx.x`, so the per-destination launches are expected to agree bit for bit with a fused launch of the same shape.

**`dst_block_size` stays a `uint16_t`.** The shared kernel layout is the CUDA struct and sizes above 65535 do not fit that field. This PR keeps the layout and validates the size on the host instead; see "Changes that affect the default path" for why that check is not ROCm-scoped.

**On ROCm, `ProcessGroupNCCL` retires the registry identity before RCCL abort or destroy, and retirement carries a generation.** NCCL2 already retired early; the stock path did not, so a retained handle could launch a barrier through a dead communicator. Retirement is the first line, and it is `USE_ROCM`-guarded at the abort and shutdown call sites. On ROCm it must also run for *aborted* comms: retirement only erases map entries and makes no RCCL call, so skipping it would leave the registry pointing at a dead communicator and cause the very deregister-through-a-dead-comm failure it was meant to avoid. Because an aborted-comm path can run from a destructor, it reads the handle through `getNcclCommUnchecked()` and uses it only as an identity token. A monotonic generation covers the remaining case: the peer-alloc object records the generation it registered under and skips destructor deregistration unless that exact registration is still live, which is what makes a successor that reuses the same `ncclComm_t` address safe.

**A stale handle is recoverable, not permanently dead.** Re-rendezvous drops a cached handle whose communicator has been replaced and rebuilds against the successor. The gate is the presence of a successor rather than staleness, because the rebuild runs a collective window registration while the liveness test is rank-local: gating on staleness would let a rank that is further along in teardown enter that collective alone. With no successor registered, every rank sees the same thing and the call raises instead. Recovery is per-rendezvous, not in-place, in two senses: a reference the caller is still holding keeps naming the retired registration and keeps raising, and recovery is only safe if every rank re-rendezvouses the same tensors in the same order.

**Liveness checks are ROCm-only.** The use-after-destroy bug is not ROCm-specific, but it surfaced here as an HSA memory fault. CUDA accessors are left unchanged on purpose. `get_window_offset()` is the existing CUDA+ROCm unification from PR #195516; this PR does not split it. It is arithmetic over two immutable members (`buffer_offset_ + offset_`), so it does not gain a liveness check. `get_offset()`, `get_buffer_size()`, `get_rank()`, `get_world_size()`, and `get_device()` are the same: scalars that cannot touch a dead communicator. Callers that then use the offset go through `get_window()` or a CFT accessor, which do check. `get_group_name()` checks as well: resolving a communicator from a name is the hazard, so the guard sits on the accessor rather than on the call sites that happen to reach it today.

**Allocation size is rounded to `NCCL_WIN_REQUIRED_ALIGNMENT` on ROCm only.** An unrounded backing allocation produced wrong `put_wait_signal` data and a teardown timeout. The registration size itself does not need to be a 4096 multiple. CUDA allocation size is not changed.

## Changes that affect the default path

Five fixes here are not under `USE_ROCM` and do change CUDA behavior. Each is a pre-existing defect in shared code that this PR restructures, or a direct consequence of one. Listing them explicitly because the rest of the PR is ROCm-scoped and a reviewer should not have to grep for the exceptions.

- **Reduce-scatter silently truncated blocks larger than 65535.** `ReduceScatterOffsetsInfo::dst_block_size` is a `uint16_t` and the host wrote `static_cast<uint16_t>(owned_sizes[j])` with no bound - the only prior check was on block *count* (`n_owned <= RS_MAX_BLOCKS_PER_RANK`). A taller shard reduced `owned_sizes[j] % 65536` rows and returned wrong data with no error. Now a host-side `TORCH_CHECK` (`nccl_reduce_scatter_offset.cu:341`), placed before the ROCm/CUDA launch split so both paths get it. Widening the field would change the shared struct layout. The inputs this rejects are exactly the ones that were already producing wrong results, so it cannot regress a correct program. It had no Python coverage at all; `test_reduce_scatter_offset_rejects_oversized_block` adds it, asserting both that the first oversized block raises and that the largest block that still fits reduces correctly.

- **Cached device comms survived a communicator replacement.** `register_comm` is last-write-wins, but a cached `ncclDevComm` is built from one specific host comm. When a successor process group registered a different comm under the same uid (restart-after-error), `get_devcomm` kept handing kernels devcomms naming a comm the registry no longer owned, and `~NCCLDevCommManager` would pass the *successor's* comm to `ncclDevCommDestroy` alongside a predecessor-built devcomm. Reachable on CUDA, which has registered under `getGroupUid()` since before this PR. `register_comm` now evicts `devcomm_registry_` on replacement (`nccl_devcomm_manager.hpp:275`); re-publishing the same pointer is not a replacement. Covered by `NCCLDevCommManagerTest.ReplacementRegistrationEvictsDevComms`, which also asserts a bystander group's devcomm survives, so a future refactor to a blanket `clear()` fails the test.

- **`get_devcomm` handed out a reference into a map it then unlocked.** `get_devcomm` and `register_devcomm` returned `std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<ncclDevComm>>` and released `mutex_` on return; both ops bound that as `ncclDevComm&` and used it as a kernel launch argument hundreds of unlocked lines later. The eviction above widens that window, so both now return `std::optional<ncclDevComm>` by value and the two call sites bind a copy (`nccl_all_to_all_nd.cu:183`, `nccl_reduce_scatter_offset.cu:218`). `ncclDevComm` is copied into the launch anyway, so this costs nothing. It is a signature change on a public-header class; `git grep` finds no other in-tree caller.

- **A late destructor could erase a live successor's registration.** `~ProcessGroupNCCL` unregistered by group uid alone (the key-only `unregister_comm` overload), so a predecessor destroyed after a same-uid successor registered would wipe the successor's entry and leave symmetric memory unable to resolve a communicator. It now goes through `unregisterSymmetricMemoryComm` (`ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:299`), which calls the identity-safe `unregister_comm(uid, comm)` - a no-op unless that exact registration is still live. That overload already existed and had no callers; this PR wires CUDA to it. One residual stays open on CUDA and is documented at the call site: `ncclComm_t` addresses are recycled, so a successor handed the predecessor's address still compares equal. Closing that needs a generation token threaded through registration, which would change `NCCLDevCommManager`'s interface and add process-group state; this PR keeps the generation ROCm-side rather than reshaping a working CUDA path. The pointer check alone is strictly better than the key-only erase it replaces.

- **The one-sided ops dereferenced an unchecked `dynamic_cast`.** `nccl_put_signal` and `nccl_wait_signal` are schema'd over the `SymmetricMemory` base class, so a handle from another backend is a legal argument, and both used the cast result without testing it - a null deref. Now `TORCH_CHECK`ed (`nccl_extension.cu:372`, `:407`), matching what the sibling ops already did. `NCCLOneSidedOpHandleTypeTest::test_one_sided_ops_reject_foreign_handle` covers it.

Also visible on CUDA, but not behavioral: `#include <vector_types.h>` is dropped from `NCCLSymmetricMemory.cu` (nothing in that translation unit references a CUDA vector type, and the header does not exist on ROCm); `ProcessGroupNCCL` gains an unconditionally-declared `symmMemCommGenerationMap_`, populated only on ROCm - declaring it behind a macro would make the class layout differ across translation units; `nccl_dev_cap.hpp` only ever *adds* ROCm terms to its conditions, so the CUDA truth value of `NCCL_HAS_SYMMEM_SUPPORT` and `NCCL_HAS_SYMMEM_DEVICE_SUPPORT` is unchanged, and the `NCCL_HAS_DEVCOMM` / `NCCL_HAS_ONE_SIDED_API` hunk merges two byte-identical `#if` conditions into one block; plus a `<limits>` include, a `[[maybe_unused]]`, and `_is_nccl_symmem_available()`, which is additive and only used by the test suite to pick a skip predicate.

## Tests

`test/distributed/test_nccl.py` no longer carries a blanket `TEST_WITH_ROCM` skip on the symmetric-memory classes. The blanket skip is replaced by three narrower, individually-justified gates, all of which are no-ops on CUDA:

- `skip_if_rccl_symmem_not_compiled` - the build-time probe result, exposed to Python as `_is_nccl_symmem_available()`.
- `skip_if_rccl_lt_2_30_4` - the RCCL host device-API floor.
- `skip_if_mi350_rocm_lt_10_1` - MI350 on pre-10.1 ROCm only, because that is where the defect reproduced.

New coverage, all of it running on the preview label:

- `NCCLSymmetricMemoryLifecycleTest` (ROCm-only, 4 items) - retirement before abort, and stale-handle recovery across a same-name restart, each on both `nccl` and `nccl-legacy` (only `nccl-legacy` goes through stock `ProcessGroupNCCL::abortCommsFromMap`).
- `NCCLSymmetricMemoryCapabilityGateTest` (ROCm-only, 3 items) - the runtime device-API snapshot, and the `TORCH_NCCL_SYMM_MEM_DISABLE_CAPTURE_ALLOC` kill switch.
- `NCCLSymmetricMemorySubgroupTest` (ROCm-only, 1 item) - subgroup-first rendezvous in a fresh process.
- `NCCLSymmetricMemoryRestartTest` (**not** ROCm-gated, 2 items) - allocation after a default-PG restart, and a successor PG surviving its predecessor's teardown.
- `NCCLOneSidedOpHandleTypeTest` (**not** ROCm-gated, 1 item) - `put_signal`/`wait_signal` reject a non-NCCL handle instead of dereferencing a null `dynamic_cast`.
- `NCCLSymmetricMemoryTest::test_reduce_scatter_offset_rejects_oversized_block` (**not** ROCm-gated) - the `uint16_t` block bound. This one also runs on the CUDA `sm90-symm` job.

Plus `NCCLDevCommManagerTest::ReplacementRegistrationEvictsDevComms` (C++, **not** ROCm-gated) - devcomm eviction on communicator replacement, that eviction does not touch a bystander group, and that a predecessor's late retirement cannot unpublish its successor. That binary is built on both platforms but is not wired into any CI script, on `main` or here; see the CUDA coverage table below.

Still skipped on ROCm, each for a named reason: `test_nccl_symmem_rendezvous_subgroup` (RCCL hangs in `ncclRmaCeInit`'s bootstrap barrier when WORLD already holds a window), `test_put_wait_signal` and `test_nccl_symmem_signal_rank_out_of_bounds` (pre-existing ROCm skip), and `SymmMemCftHandleTest` (host-side CFT is not this PR).

## Validation

All numbers below are read out of the uploaded `test-reports` XML for the shard that owns `distributed/test_nccl.py` on this PR's head [`9f74504`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/9f7745040cdcb3857b0cf891a843c23162d64379) (merge base `d90134f`), not from a local run. The file collects **52 items** on all four ROCm labels.

| Label / job | GPU | ROCm | `test_nccl.py` result |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ciflow/rocm-preview](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35176227575) `linux-noble-rocm-preview-py3.12-mi350` | gfx950 | 10.1 | **47 passed, 5 skipped** |
| [ciflow/trunk](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35176229226) `linux-jammy-rocm-py3.10-mi350` | gfx950 | 10.0 | 52 skipped |
| [ciflow/periodic-rocm-mi300](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35176233963) `linux-noble-rocm-py3.12-mi300` | gfx942 | 10.0 | 52 skipped |
| [ciflow/periodic-rocm-mi200](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35176228056) `linux-jammy-rocm-py3.10-mi200` | gfx90a | 10.0 | 52 skipped |

### Preview is the only label with live coverage, and why

47 passed on gfx950 / ROCm 10.1 / RCCL 2.30.7. The 5 skips are the ones this PR deliberately keeps: `test_nccl_symmem_rendezvous_subgroup`, `test_put_wait_signal`, `test_nccl_symmem_signal_rank_out_of_bounds`, and the two `SymmMemCftHandleTest` cases.

The three ROCm 10.0 labels skip, but **not all for the same reason**, and the difference is the point:

| Label | Skip reason in the XML | Count |
|---|---|---|
| trunk mi350 | `MI350 symmetric memory requires ROCm 10.1 or newer` | 50 |
| trunk mi350 | ` NCCL_HAS_HOST_CFT (nccl_dev_cap.hpp:51-54) needs NCCL >=2.31.2` | 2 |
| mi300 / mi200 | `RCCL symmetric memory was disabled at build time; nccl_device.h did not pass the host-translation-unit compatibility probe` | 47 |
| mi300 / mi200 | `Capture-time symmetric allocation requires RCCL 2.30.7 or newer` | 3 |
| mi300 / mi200 | ` NCCL_HAS_HOST_CFT (nccl_dev_cap.hpp:51-54) needs NCCL >=2.31.2` | 2 |

Narrowing the version floor from a blanket ROCm gate to an MI350-only one did what it was meant to: MI200 and MI300 no longer skip on a version floor. They now fall through to the build-time gate, and that gate is the binding constraint - the `nccl_device.h` in those images does not compile in a host translation unit, so the feature is compiled out of the binary entirely and no test-side predicate can produce coverage there. Widening coverage past preview is therefore a matter of the periodic ROCm images carrying a qualifying RCCL, not of test gating.

trunk mi350 is the useful control for the remaining floor: it is the *same gfx950 hardware* as preview, on a ROCm 10.0 container, and it skips on exactly the MI350 predicate. That is the intended behavior of the narrowed gate.

### CUDA coverage for the default-path changes

Of the five, only the first is exercised by CUDA CI on this head. Spelling out the rest rather than leaving it implied, since the whole point of the section above is that a ROCm-labelled PR is touching a shared path.

| Change | CUDA CI on this head |
|---|---|
| Reduce-scatter block bound | **Runs and passes.** `test_reduce_scatter_offset_rejects_oversized_block` executed on `sm90-symm` under both CUDA [13.0](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35176226367/job/105062525291) and [13.2](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35176226367/job/105063072045) - 35 collected, 2 skipped, neither of them this one. It sits in `NCCLSymmetricMemoryTest`, which is what `.ci/pytorch/test.sh:559` filters for. Not skipping also proves those images carry NCCL >= 2.29.7. |
| Devcomm eviction on replacement | Asserted by `NCCLDevCommManagerTest.ReplacementRegistrationEvictsDevComms`, which is outside the file's `#ifdef USE_ROCM` and builds on CUDA - but **no CI script runs the binary**, on any platform. It is compiled, installed to `build/bin`, and unpacked on the test runner; the hardcoded C++ list at `.ci/pytorch/test.sh:1780-1782` does not include it. |
| `get_devcomm` by value | No dedicated test. It is a lifetime fix with no observable behavior change, exercised implicitly by any all-to-all or reduce-scatter. |
| Identity-safe unregister | Same gtest, final assertion (`unregister_comm(group, first)` then `get_comm(group) == successor`), deliberately written to need only CUDA-available accessors. Same gap: never invoked. |
| One-sided `dynamic_cast` checks | **No CUDA coverage.** `test_one_sided_ops_reject_foreign_handle` is in `NCCLOneSidedOpHandleTypeTest`, which the `-k NCCLSymmetricMemoryTest` filter excludes from the H100 job; the only other CUDA job that collects the file runs on T4, where `@requires_cuda_p2p_access()` skips all 52 items. |

Two one-line CI changes would close the gap - widening that `-k` to `"NCCLSymmetricMemoryTest or NCCLOneSidedOpHandleTypeTest"`, and adding `cpp/NCCLDevCommManagerTest` to the C++ distributed list. Both are edits to shared CI config rather than to this feature, and the gtest has never run in CI before, so I would rather do them in a separate PR than widen this one's blast radius. Happy to fold them in here if you would rather have the coverage land with the change it covers.

Locally, all 11 cases pass on gfx950 / ROCm 10.1:

```
$ build/bin/NCCLDevCommManagerTest
[==========] 11 tests from 1 test suite ran. (2958 ms total)
[  PASSED  ] 11 tests.
```

Three of those are `#ifdef USE_ROCM` (the generation-token cases); the other eight, including the two that cover the changes above, are what a CUDA build would run.

### Unrelated CI failures

Six jobs are red on this head. None of them runs a test that reaches this PR's changed files, and four are artifacts of a merge base that predates two unrelated CI changes on `main`.

### Measurements CI does not reproduce

The two-arm allocation digest comparison, the in-capture alloc/rendezvous/replay probe, and the per-config reduce-scatter kernel comparison were run on an 8x MI355X box (HIP 7.16.26344, RCCL 2.30.7, `torch.version.rocm` 10.1.0). They are recorded in the evidence notes and available on request.

Fixes #168480

body:
Fixes #198545

`TritonOverrides.floordiv` negates both operands when the divisor is negative, and negating the minimum value overflows back to itself, so `iinfo.min // b` had the wrong sign for every `b < 0`. For `b < 0` and `a == min` this divides `a - b` instead and adds 1.

title: [ROCm] Expose shared_memory_per_block_optin
body:
## Summary

`torch.cuda.get_device_properties()` exposes
`shared_memory_per_block_optin` on NVIDIA, but the binding is excluded from
ROCm builds. HIP provides the same limit as
`hipDeviceProp_t::sharedMemPerBlockOptin`.

Expose the property on ROCm 6.0 and newer, where the field is present in the
HIP device-properties structure. Older ROCm builds remain unchanged.

Remove comments that describe the property as NVIDIA-only. Inductor's existing
property check is unchanged; once the binding is available, it naturally reads
the opt-in limit on ROCm. The profiler export can also include the value through
its existing `hasattr()` guard.

This PR only exposes the property. Replacing hardcoded shared-memory limits in
downstream consumers is a separate follow-up.

## Validation

`test_cuda_shared_memory_per_block_optin` is the regression guard. On current
main it fails on ROCm because the property is missing. With this change it is
present and no smaller than the default per-block limit.

| Device | Base limit | Opt-in limit |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | 65536 | 65536 |
| gfx1151 | 65536 | 65536 |
| gfx1200 | 65536 | 65536 |

An independent HIP probe also confirmed that
`hipDeviceProp_t::sharedMemPerBlockOptin` matches
`hipDeviceAttributeSharedMemPerBlockOptin` on all three devices.

The test skips ROCm versions older than 6.0, matching the source guard. This
work is scoped to RDNA; ROCm CI should cover MI architectures.
