title: [inductor][NVGEMM] Chain dependent NVFP4 launches into Triton consumers
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #197485
* #194651
* #194652
* #194649

Human commentary: Provider-side dependent launch only helps when the direct consumer participates, so I want one reviewable change that carries the protocol across the complete launch chain.

AI-assisted content:

> ## Problem
>
> Fixes #198174
> Fixes #198175
>
> NVGEMM kernels could not participate in CUDA programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so direct Triton consumers waited for ordinary kernel completion instead of overlapping their launch setup with the producer tail.
>
> ## Summary
>
> Add selective PDL for measured NVFP4 decode shapes and connect eligible NVGEMM providers to direct same-stream Triton consumers.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> The NVGEMM heuristics module owns the complete shape policy. In `"auto"` mode it generates PDL-capable operators only for NVFP4 1x16 problems with `0 < M <= 256` and logical `N` and `K` in `[1024, 65536]`, excluding the measured regression band `32 < M <= 64` and `2048 < min(N, K) < 4096`. `"0"` disables PDL, while `"1"` forces it for experiments. The policy receives packed FP4 K from `MMKernelInputs` and performs the packed-to-logical conversion internally.
>
> The selected policy is represented in operator metadata and included in generated-precompile, runtime, and persistent-artifact cache identities. Original logical M is also part of specialization when swap-AB changes the physical orientation.
>
> Inside the CuTeDSL provider, PDL waits before consuming dependency-produced inputs and releases dependent grids while its output stores drain; the consumer wait prevents dependent reads until completion and visibility. For measured small-K decode shapes, descriptor and layout setup is moved before the wait so independent prologue work overlaps; other shapes retain the conservative early wait.
>
> Scheduler code generation tracks the previous concrete scheduler node independently per device and stream. A Triton launch opts into PDL only when the immediately preceding same-stream node resolves to a selected PDL-capable NVGEMM and the consumer has a true read-after-write dependency on its output. Composite launches, multi-kernel wrappers, workspaces, unsupported reductions, cross-stream consumers, and unrelated nodes retain ordinary launch behavior.
>
> ## Examples
>
> - An eligible NVFP4 decode projection followed directly on the same stream by a Triton cast or add launches the consumer with `launch_pdl` and waits through `gdc_wait`.
> - A consumer on another stream behind an event, or one separated by an unrelated same-stream kernel, uses ordinary stream/event ordering and receives no PDL launch attribute.
>
> ## Performance
>
> Standard `vllm bench latency` runs on GB200 used 32 input tokens, 128 output tokens, 10 warmups, 30 samples, `-O2`, static compilation/CUDA graphs, dummy weights, and tuned FlashInfer 0.6.18.post1 as control. Only vLLM's per-quant `nvfp4_w4a4` linear backend changed; unrelated linears, attention, and sampling remained matched.
>
> These are cumulative complete-stack results, not isolated attribution to this PR:
>
> - Llama-3.1-8B NVFP4: Torch/NVGEMM was 7.81%, 7.42%, 8.29%, and 7.83% faster than tuned FlashInfer at batches 8, 32, 64, and 128.
> - Qwen3-14B NVFP4: Torch/NVGEMM was 5.15%, 5.67%, 7.87%, and 5.23% faster at batches 8, 32, 64, and 128.
> - Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 NVFP4: Torch/NVGEMM was 3.81% and 2.04% faster at batches 32 and 64, and nominally 0.46% faster at batch 128, which is treated as parity/a close result.
> - A Llama batch-64 PDL ablation improved the midpoint of two PDL medians by 7.27% over the intervening no-PDL run. Forced PDL improved four isolated Nemotron decode GEMMs by 11.1%--13.2%; automatic policy excludes the nearby end-to-end regression band.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> ```bash
> python test/inductor/test_nv_universal_gemm.py -k pdl
> lintrunner -a
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> Tests cover policy boundaries, PDL candidate preference and fallback, provider wait/release placement, logical-shape cache specialization, pointer refresh, direct same-stream dependencies, cross-stream event ordering, reductions, deferred copies, composite launches, multi-kernel wrappers, and workspaces.
>
> ## Checklist
>
> - [x] Passes lint
> - [x] Added or updated tests
> - [x] Updated documentation where applicable
> - [x] Included benchmark results
>
> ## BC-breaking?
>
> No. Automatic PDL is shape-scoped; `TORCHINDUCTOR_NVGEMM_PDL=0` and `=1` remain explicit overrides.
>
> PR prepared with assistance from an AI tool.

title: [inductor][NVGEMM] Improve NVFP4 autotuning
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #197485
* #194651
* __->__ #194652
* #194649

Human commentary: Short NVFP4 inference GEMMs need a small automatic candidate set and measurements that reflect transformer decode execution.

AI-assisted content:

> ## Problem
>
> Fixes #198172
>
> `nvMatmulHeuristics` does not cover several Blackwell NVFP4 decode winners, while an unrestricted supplemental pool adds substantial compile and profiling cost. The related shape rules were also split between code generation and candidate filtering, which made the policy difficult to audit.
>
> ## Summary
>
> Add a bounded, shape-aware NVFP4 candidate policy for Blackwell decode workloads and centralize every NVFP4 shape decision in the NVGEMM heuristics module.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> `torch/_inductor/heuristics/template/nv_universal_gemm.py` is the single policy boundary. It identifies the NVFP4 1x16 recipe, decides when to expose swap-AB, chooses the CUDA-graph replay count and cold-weight scope, applies the profiling cap, and returns the shape-scoped primary and prefetch candidate keys. The codegen integration passes problem metadata to these helpers but contains no independent shape cutoffs.
>
> The ranked `nvMatmulHeuristics` result remains the primary pool. Successful heuristic ranking is capped at three candidates in each ordinary and epilogue-fusion-capable (EFC) pool by default; fallback, supplemental, and wide-tile paths may add more. Within measured shape ranges, the centralized policy adds missing narrow-N decode tactics, medium-M native and swapped tactics, selected prefetch variants, and a large-M 256x192 tile with a 2x2 cluster. Candidate keys are deduplicated, unranked fallback paths retain primary non-prefetch variants, and dynamic-N problems exclude tactics that require a known narrow N. Explicit controls can still request fewer candidates or an exhaustive supplemental search.
>
> NVGEMM-only decode requests use 16 CUDA-graph replays and rotate weight, scale, and output buffers to avoid permanently L2-hot selection. Mixed-backend decisions in this PR retain the shared global policy; the next PR uses the opt-in hook added here to apply one override to every choice. Runtime EFC lookup also retains the GEMM's pre-fusion output dtype, avoiding reconstruction of the full operator manifest for output-cast fusions.
>
> ## Examples
>
> - Logical `M=32, N=4096` NVFP4 projections add the measured transposed 32/64-wide tactics that `nvMatmulHeuristics` misses.
> - Logical `M=128` projections admit the measured 128x64 and 128x128 prefetch variants. FP8, MXFP4, and BF16 keep their ordinary policy; dynamic-N NVFP4 excludes narrow-N tactics and uses only candidates valid without a concrete N.
>
> ## Performance
>
> On the later complete stack with the final selective-PDL policy, changing only the ranked-family cap from five to three preserved or improved selected-kernel latency for all 15 shapes. It reduced aggregate candidate time from 189.03 s to 164.93 s (12.75%). A Qwen3-14B batch-32 run reduced NVGEMM tuning from 49.684 s to 40.738 s (18.0%); its 0.10% end-to-end change was below unlocked-clock run spread.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> ```bash
> python test/inductor/test_nv_universal_gemm.py -k TestNVUniversalGemmHeuristics
> lintrunner -a
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> Focused source-loaded policy execution covered 55 cases for recipe detection, swap-AB, replay/cold-cache boundaries, profiling caps, supplemental and prefetch candidate tables, fallback ordering, dynamic N, MXFP4 exclusion, and PDL-independent integration behavior.
>
> ## Checklist
>
> - [x] Passes lint
> - [x] Added or updated tests
> - [x] Updated documentation where applicable
> - [x] Included benchmark results
>
> ## BC-breaking?
>
> No user-facing BC. The ranked-family cap applies recipe-wide to NVFP4 1x16; swap-AB, replay, cold-cache rotation, and supplemental tactics remain shape-scoped.
>
> PR prepared with assistance from an AI tool.

title: [ROCm][c10d] Enable NCCL2 reconfigure on ROCm
body:
## Summary

Enable nccl2 communicator reconfigure on ROCm by dropping the `USE_ROCM` compile-time exclusion around `ncclCommRevoke` and `supportsReconfigure()`.

Version gates:

- CUDA: unchanged, NCCL 2.28.0
- ROCm: RCCL 2.30.4 (first released RCCL with `ncclCommRevoke`, ROCm 7.14)


## Timeout-retry / RCCL hang

`Nccl2FaultToleranceTest` no longer has a class-level ROCm skip. `test_reconfigure_timeout_is_retryable` runs on ROCm 10.1 and newer and is skipped below that with `skipIfRocmVersionLessThan((10, 1))` (ROCM-30165).

Stock RCCL 2.30.4 hangs on the missing-rank nonblocking init path used by that test (`ncclGroupEndInternal` still inspects emptied `ncclAsyncJobs` after jobs were moved to `groupJob->asyncJobs`). The RCCL fix is in [ROCm/rocm-systems#10796](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/pull/10796) (`7621e6c`, 2026-08-28). It is **not** in ROCm 10.0 / RCCL 2.30.4. The first 10.1 nightly that includes it is `10.1.0a20260901`; this PR was checked against `10.1.0a20260902`.

These tests use `world_size = 3` and skip unless `torch.cuda.device_count() >= 3`, so typical 2-GPU ROCm distributed jobs never enter this class. On 3+ GPU runners with ROCm 10.0, the version skip keeps the test from hanging.

## Test plan

- [x] Local 3-GPU MI355X (`gfx950`) against `rocm==10.1.0a20260902` / RCCL 2.30.7 at `ccbac3faaec`
  - `Nccl2FaultToleranceTest.test_reconfigure_timeout_is_retryable`: ok in 4.647s (previously hung on RCCL 2.30.4 until OS timeout)
  - `test/distributed/test_c10d_fault_tolerance.py`: 34 tests, OK, 3 expected Gloo skips
- [x] Rebased onto `main` (`69f2e45ef34`). The only change since the validated SHA is the ROCm < 10.1 skip. On ROCm 10.2 (`torch.version.rocm = 10.2.0`) the skip does not fire; with the version patched to 10.0 it does.
- [ ] CI on `ffd2d4738b4`

title: [dynamo] Reject a zero range step at construction
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. In plain Python, `range(1, 2, 0)` raises `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` right at the `range()` call. Under `torch.compile`, a function that only creates this range inside `try/except ValueError` returned as if nothing was wrong, which hides the real error. A function that uses the range, `list(range(1, 2, 0))`, crashed with `InternalTorchDynamoError` instead, even without `fullgraph`, so the `except ValueError` could not catch it. With this PR compiled code raises the same `ValueError` at the `range()` call as eager.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (reject a zero `range` step at construction).
>
> `BuiltinVariable.call_range` converted the arguments to indices with `pynumber_index` but built a `RangeVariable` without checking for a zero step, while CPython raises `ValueError` in the `range()` call itself. It now checks the converted step when it is a Python constant and raises an observed `ValueError` with CPython's message. This placement has access to the tracing transaction, unlike validation inside `RangeVariable`, and lets a surrounding handler catch the error.
>
> **Tests**
>
> - `test_functions.py::test_range_zero_step`: under `fullgraph=True`, `range(1, 2, step)` inside `try/except ValueError` matches eager for step `0` (the handler runs) and step `2` (no error). Fails without the fix.
>
> CPython `test_range` under Dynamo: `RangeTest.test_invalid_invocation` goes from error to passing and no test goes from passing to failing; its expected-failure marker is removed. The other tests in `test/dynamo/test_functions.py` show the same results with and without the change.
>
> ```
> TORCHINDUCTOR_WINDOWS_TESTS=1 python test/dynamo/test_functions.py -v -k test_range_zero_step
> TORCHINDUCTOR_WINDOWS_TESTS=1 python test/dynamo/test_functions.py -v
> PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_range.py -v
> ```
>
> Tested locally on Windows, Python 3.13, with a matching nightly build; other platforms and Python versions are left to CI.

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Keep NVIDIA reduction thresholds off HIP
body:
## Summary

Two reduction heuristics use the device major version as an NVIDIA SM version:

- the inner-reduction no-split threshold selects GB200 values for `major >= 10`
- the `R0_BLOCK` architecture cap selects the B200 value for `major >= 10`

ROCm reports the `gfx` major in the same field, so gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200
are incorrectly treated as SM100+ hardware.

Limit the no-split thresholds to normalized `DeviceProperties.type == "cuda"`.
For `R0_BLOCK`, keep the NVIDIA condition in the base heuristic and override
only the architecture cap in `ROCmReductionHeuristic`. Workload-specific caps
remain unchanged.

The strided-block test helper now constructs the `DeviceProperties` type
required by the threshold function instead of passing raw CUDA properties.

## Validation

The two regression tests use synthetic `DeviceProperties`, following the
existing reduction-heuristic test style.

`test_inner_reduction_no_split_threshold_is_nvidia_only` checks:

- HIP major 12 returns the default 8192
- CUDA major 12 retains 32768/40960
- a missing major returns 8192

`test_reduction_r0_block_cap_is_nvidia_only` checks:

- CUDA major 8 returns 2048
- CUDA major 10 returns the B200 cap of 1024
- ROCm major 12 returns 2048
- ROCm major 9 remains 2048

On current main, the HIP no-split assertion returns 32768 instead of 8192 and
the ROCm major-12 R0 assertion returns 1024 instead of 2048. Both tests pass
after the change and run without requiring ROCm hardware.

Separate real-device probes confirmed the same values:

| Device | Value | Current main | With this change |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | no-split threshold | 32768 | 8192 |
| gfx1100 | first `R0_BLOCK` | 1024 | 2048 |
| gfx1151 | no-split threshold | 32768 | 8192 |
| gfx1151 | first `R0_BLOCK` | 1024 | 2048 |
| gfx1200 | no-split threshold | 32768 | 8192 |
| gfx1200 | first `R0_BLOCK` | 1024 | 2048 |

This work is scoped to RDNA. ROCm CI should cover MI architectures.

title: [inductor][NVGEMM] Fuse NVFP4 output scaling
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #197485
* __->__ #194651
* #194652
* #194649

Human commentary: ModelOpt NVFP4 linear layers multiply `_scaled_mm` output by a scalar dequantization factor. Folding that factor before QKV fan-out removes one standalone scale launch per layer and lets autotuning consider the GEMM implementation that applies it directly.

AI-assisted content:

> ## Problem
>
> Fixes #198173
>
> ModelOpt NVFP4 linears materialize a separate pointwise multiply after `_scaled_mm`. That launch is especially visible during decode. Waiting until scheduler fusion is too late for two reasons: GEMM candidates have already been constructed, so native NVGEMM output scaling cannot participate in autotuning; and a QKV split/view fan-out no longer looks like one simple pointwise suffix that the scheduler can attach to a single producer.
>
> ## Summary
>
> Fold eligible NVFP4 output scaling into the selected scaled-matmul implementation while preserving semantically equivalent ATen fallback choices and tensor-parallel transformations.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> A post-grad graph pattern recognizes `aten._scaled_mm(...) * output_scale` in either multiply order. Post-grad is the earliest existing boundary that has the required graph structure while still preceding lowering, candidate construction, and scheduling. Rewriting there exposes native-alpha NVGEMM candidates to the autotuner instead of trying to modify the already-selected kernel later.
>
> The QKV case is the main fan-out rationale. The original graph contains one multiply before `chunk`/split/view consumers. Folding it into the GEMM produces the already-scaled buffer consumed by every branch and removes that one standalone launch per layer. If the multiply survives until scheduling, moving it through the multi-consumer fan-out would require a separate cross-consumer transformation; ordinary single-consumer epilogue fusion cannot recover the same result. Conversely, a complete pointwise suffix with no such boundary remains untouched so the scheduler can use its existing epilogue fusion.
>
> The predicate accepts packed FP4 inputs with E4M3 1x16 block scales and a zero-dimensional CUDA FP32 multiplier. Pattern structure excludes existing bias and public `scale_result`; the predicate rejects fast accumulation, shared GEMM output, incompatible scale recipes, pipelined autotuning, and tensor-parallel structures that the micro-pipeline pass can consume.
>
> The rewritten node carries the scale tensor through IR, candidate construction, subprocess precompile metadata, cache specialization, swap-AB, and runtime pointer refresh. The vendored block-scaled NVGEMM provider advertises native output-scale support explicitly. For mixed `ATEN,NVGEMM` tuning, an ATen extern candidate performs `_scaled_mm` followed by multiply under the same replay and cold-buffer policy. If every native folded choice fails, lowering restores the ordinary scaled matmul and multiply.
>
> ## Examples
>
> ```python
> out = torch._scaled_mm(
>     a, b, scale_a=sa, scale_b=sb, out_dtype=torch.bfloat16
> )
> q, k, v = (out * output_scale).chunk(3, dim=-1)
> ```
>
> When an NVGEMM choice wins, the scale becomes that provider's alpha before the split/view fan-out. A direct all-gather form eligible for micro-pipeline tensor parallelism is left unchanged; unsupported or reshaped collective forms may use the fold.
>
> ## Performance
>
> On GB200 with Llama-3.1-8B NVFP4 at batch 64, the fold removes 32 launches per decode step and reduces the captured graph from 481 to 449 nodes. The later complete stack measured representative graph spans of 2.175--2.180 ms versus 2.232--2.237 ms before the fold; those span numbers also include later PDL overlap and are not isolated attribution to this PR. Candidate selection remains the larger source of the complete-stack speedup; this PR removes the residual per-layer scale launch and makes the native scaled candidate selectable.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> ```bash
> python test/inductor/test_nv_universal_gemm.py -k output_scale
> python test/distributed/tensor/parallel/test_micro_pipeline_tp.py -k test_scaled_mm_output_scale_preserves_all_gather_fusion
> lintrunner -a
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> Focused validation on GB200 passed 8 output-scale tests and 3 tensor-parallel preservation tests after test consolidation. Coverage includes both multiply orders, QKV split/view fan-out, pointwise-versus-nonpointwise consumer boundaries, fast-accum rejection, public `scale_result`, MXFP4 exclusion, shared outputs, native-choice fallback, the generated runtime path, worker-precompile serialization, and tensor-parallel preservation.
>
> ## Checklist
>
> - [x] Passes lint
> - [x] Added or updated tests
> - [x] Updated documentation where applicable
> - [x] Included benchmark results
>
> ## BC-breaking?
>
> No. Ineligible patterns continue through ordinary lowering.
>
> PR prepared with assistance from an AI tool.

title: [Inductor] Add a Gluon template frontend, first used by flex_attention on gfx950
body:
Following up on RFC (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188212) 

Adds Gluon — Triton's low-level frontend — as a template frontend for Inductor, and uses it to offer a hand-tuned flash-attention forward kernel as an extra `flex_attention` autotuning candidate on gfx950. Gluon exposes explicit tile layouts and target intrinsics, so the kernel can stage K/V from global to LDS by DMA and keep that transfer in flight across the MFMAs — an overlap Inductor's Triton codegen cannot currently express. Worth 1.08x to 1.12x on the forward pass, and the frontend is reusable by anything else that wants a hand-written body.

MI350X, ROCm 7.2.1, fp16, forward only, TFLOPS:

| shape | mask | triton | gluon | ratio |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| B1 H16 N4096 D64 | none | 514.0 | 574.0 | 1.117x |
| B1 H16 N4096 D64 | causal | 316.3 | 348.7 | 1.102x |
| B1 H16 N4096 D128 | none | 620.6 | 687.3 | 1.107x |
| B1 H16 N4096 D128 | causal | 398.2 | 434.5 | 1.091x |
| B1 H32 N8192 D128 | none | 640.6 | 713.6 | 1.114x |
| B1 H32 N8192 D128 | causal | 469.3 | 509.7 | 1.086x |

Geomean 1.103x, against a worst-case measurement drift of 0.4%.

This also lays the groundwork for the next generation (gfx1250 / CDNA5), where the gap Gluon can close tends to be widest: each generation adds mechanisms a codegen has to learn to model — async copy here, warp specialization and TMA/mbarrier there — and Gluon exposes them immediately. A body that does not win the autotune never runs, so offering one costs nothing where Triton is already at the ceiling.

<details>
<summary>How the numbers were taken</summary>

Both arms are compiled in one process and timed A/B/A, so drift within the run shows up as a difference between the two Triton measurements rather than as a Gluon effect; the worst such drift was 0.3% and the Gluon spread 0.1% to 0.6%. Each point is the median of five `do_bench` medians after a clock ramp, and each figure above is the median of three such runs on a device checked idle before each. This is a shared host: one of the three runs picked up a transient co-tenant that cost the first shape 3.5% before it recovered on repeat, which is what taking medians across runs is for.

The baseline has to remove the Gluon choices from the pool rather than merely stop forcing them. Leave them in and Gluon wins the baseline autotune too, and the comparison reads 1.00x.

</details>

### The frontend

`torch/_inductor/codegen/gluon` is target-neutral and knows nothing about attention.

`GluonTemplate` / `GluonTemplateKernel` subclass `TritonTemplate` / `TritonTemplateKernel` and override only the emitted imports and the jit decorator. Signature generation, `modification()` subgraph rendering, `store_output`, argument plumbing and the kernel call are all inherited, and `TritonScheduling` and `async_compile.triton` are reused as they are. That works because `GluonJITFunction` subclasses `triton.runtime.jit.JITFunction` and launches identically, and because `tl.*` pointwise ops are valid inside a `@gluon.jit` body with layouts inferred from the operands.

This is deliberately not a backend in the shape of the landed CuteDSL one, which brings its own `BaseScheduling`, `Kernel` and modification wrapper. CuteDSL needs that because it is a different language; Gluon is not, so reusing Triton's path is what makes `score_mod`/`mask_mod` work here for free rather than needing to be reimplemented.

`GluonKernelOverrides` is the one codegen adjustment. Gluon's `gl.full` / `gl.zeros` need an explicit layout that generated subgraph code has no way to pick, since the right layout depends on the tile the constant is combined with, so constants become typed scalars that broadcast against any layout while keeping the dtype pinned.

A target contributes only its intrinsics and its wavefront width — `codegen/gluon/cdna4.py` is 24 lines. Gluon's primitives differ by family (CDNA4 has mfma and `buffer_load_to_shared`, gfx1250 has wmma and mbarrier, NVIDIA has mma and TMA), so bodies are per target while everything above them is shared. And because `score_mod`/`mask_mod` go through the inherited `modification()` machinery, arbitrary user mods work in a Gluon body with no extra support code.

### The first consumer

The flex pieces plug in through the existing `InductorChoices.append_flex_attention_choices` seam, so Gluon kernels are appended alongside the Triton candidates and the autotuner picks the winner; where the Gluon body is slower it loses and never runs. Two bodies are offered per config and autotuned against each other: a synchronous one, and an async one that stages K/V through `buffer_load_to_shared` into a double-buffered LDS ring, waiting with `wait_group(NUM_BUF - 1)` so the next block's transfer stays in flight during this block's math. The async body wins on all six shapes above.

A `GluonFlexTarget` descriptor carries the matmul tile geometry, the wavefront width and the DMA staging ladder, and the staging layouts are a table keyed by `(head_dim, BLOCK_N, num_warps)` rather than a branch chain in the template, so the choices hook and the body cannot disagree.

Off by default behind `config.gluon_flex_attention`, and gated to gfx950 on top of that.

### Preconditions the hook enforces

**`BLOCK_N` must divide `KV_LEN`.** Staging by unmasked DMA means a prefetch that would overrun the tensor is clamped to `KV_LEN - BLOCK_N`, which is a block start only under that condition. Otherwise the clamp fires on a block that is actually read, and the final block scores staged rows against another block's column indices — wrong rather than imprecise, 33% relative error at S=4000, and selected by ordinary autotuning rather than needing to be forced.

The existing `IS_DIVISIBLE` cannot express this. It is computed against `SPARSE_KV_BLOCK_SIZE`, which is `1073741824` on the unmasked path, so it is `False` both where the async body is correct and where it is not. Anything the gate rejects, including a dynamic `KV_LEN`, takes the sync body or Triton.

**The scale must be positive** for the identity `score_mod` fold, which subtracts `max(qk) * QK_SCALE` rather than the row max of the scaled scores. A negative scale makes those the row min; softmax is invariant to the constant it subtracts, but the exp2 arguments then grow with the score span and overflow to NaN past fp32's range of 128, which `scale=-1.0` at head dim 128 reaches at 145. The Triton template scales the tile first and so is sign-agnostic.

**A caller-pinned `num_warps` or `num_stages`** suppresses the Gluon offer rather than being silently rewritten, since these bodies choose their own.

### Coverage

`TestGluonFlexAttention` is skipped unless running on gfx950. The forcing tests assert a Gluon kernel was actually emitted, since otherwise a green test would only prove the Triton template still works. Correctness was additionally validated out of tree across 120 combinations of shape, `score_mod` and dtype at sequence lengths to 8192, and the sync body at head dims 16 through 256.

Forward only; the backward pass keeps using the Triton template. The async body needs `BLOCK_N=64`, head dim 64 or 128, and a `KV_LEN` that `BLOCK_N` divides, with everything else falling back to the sync body or Triton.

title: [dynamo] Use type-level __round__ lookup for user objects
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. `round()` looks for `__round__` on the class, not on the object. For an object that only has `__round__` attached to itself (`box.__round__ = lambda *a: 42`), plain Python raises `TypeError: type Box doesn't define __round__ method`, but compiled code returned `42`. That is a silent wrong result: Dynamo looked at the object instead of the class. With this PR compiled code raises the same `TypeError` as eager.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (raise `TypeError` when `round()` has no type-level `__round__`).
>
> `BuiltinVariable.call_round` fetched `__round__` with an ordinary `getattr` on the instance. That let an instance-only `__round__` attribute supply a result, even though CPython's `round()` uses the special-method lookup on the type and raises `TypeError` when the method is absent there. For `UserDefinedObjectVariable` it now uses the existing type-MRO lookup with descriptor binding (`_maybe_lookup_method`) and raises CPython's `TypeError` when nothing is found. This is narrower than changing the generic `getattr` behavior and avoids duplicating the special-method lookup; other argument types keep the existing path.
>
> **Tests**
>
> - `test_functions.py::test_round_uses_type_method`: under `fullgraph=True`, an object with only an instance-level `__round__` raises `TypeError`, and when both the class and the instance define `__round__`, the class method is used. Fails without the fix.

title: [dynamo] Probe setdefault keys only once
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. The key class counts its `__hash__` and `__eq__` calls, and all keys hash to the same value. In plain Python, `d.setdefault(key, 7)` with a missing key calls `__hash__` once and `__eq__` once. Under `torch.compile` the returned value and the dict length were right, but the missing key had `__hash__` called twice and `__eq__` twice. That is a silent wrong result: Dynamo ran `setdefault` as if it were two steps, a lookup followed by a separate insert. With this PR the counts match eager.

_(My comment above was assembled from my own notes while reviewing this change and translated from Turkish with AI assistance.)_

> **AI-generated technical summary (Claude), reviewed by me:**
>
> Part of #195901 (hash a `setdefault` key only once).
>
> `ConstDictVariable.dict_setdefault` looked the key up and then inserted it as separate `HashableTracker` operations. With a colliding user-defined key, a missing key had `__hash__` and `__eq__` each called twice, and a present key had `__eq__` called twice. CPython's `dict.setdefault` does a single probe for both lookup and insertion (bpo-13521), so eager and compiled code disagreed on how often these methods ran. It now calls `setdefault` on the backing dict with one `HashableTracker` and records a mutation only if the dict grew. Reusing one tracker across two separate probes would still repeat the equality comparisons.
>
> Scope: returned values and dict contents were already correct. The difference is only visible when `__hash__` or `__eq__` has side effects (counting, logging) or is expensive.
>
> **Tests**
>
> - `test_dicts.py::test_setdefault_hashes_and_compares_once` (parametrized: missing key / present key): under `fullgraph=True`, the returned value, dict length, per-key `__hash__` counts and total `__eq__` count match eager. Both cases fail without the fix.
>
> CPython `test_dict` under Dynamo: `DictTest.test_setdefault_atomic` goes from error to passing and no test goes from passing to failing in `test_dict`, `test_ordered_dict`, `test_userdict` or `test_defaultdict`; its expected-failure marker is removed. The other tests in `test/dynamo/test_dicts.py` show the same results with and without the change.
>
> ```
> TORCHINDUCTOR_WINDOWS_TESTS=1 python test/dynamo/test_dicts.py -v -k test_setdefault_hashes_and_compares_once
> TORCHINDUCTOR_WINDOWS_TESTS=1 python test/dynamo/test_dicts.py -v

title: [inductor] Make CUDA graph autotuning measurements consistent
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #197485
* #194651
* #194652
* __->__ #194649

Human commentary: I want every candidate in an autotune decision measured under the same launch policy so the selected kernel reflects production execution.

AI-assisted content:

> ## Problem
>
> Fixes #198171
>
> Autotune requests can be created under one Inductor configuration and executed later in another process. Without carrying the effective CUDA-graph policy on the request, candidates from the same decision can be timed under different launch conditions. CUTLASS closures also used to capture a stream too early, before CUDA graph capture selected its stream.
>
> ## Summary
>
> Make CUDA-graph autotuning policy request-scoped and consistent across current-process, subprocess, extern, Triton, and CUTLASS benchmark paths.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> `BenchmarkRequest` snapshots the effective max-autotune and automatic CUDA-graph settings when the compiler creates it. Those values are serialized with the request, applied while a worker runs it, and included in the timing-cache namespace together with the effective eager/automatic/required graph mode and replay count.
>
> The shared GPU benchmark path owns device selection, CUDA-graph replay unrolling, and optional rotation of cold inputs and outputs. It finds the GPU from all input and output metadata, captures the requested number of launches, rotates independent buffers when requested, and reports normalized per-launch time. Extern and generated-kernel callers use this path so candidates in one decision are comparable.
>
> CUTLASS benchmark closures resolve the raw CUDA stream at invocation time. During graph capture the launch therefore uses the active capture stream, rather than a stream saved when the closure was constructed. A capture failure remains an ordinary failed candidate; this change does not add an eager-retry or CUDA-worker-recovery protocol.
>
> ## Examples
>
> - A request created with automatic CUDA-graph benchmarking enabled retains that policy after serialization into an autotune worker whose process defaults differ.
> - A replay count of 16 captures 16 kernel invocations and normalizes the replay duration per invocation. CUTLASS obtains the stream immediately before each launch.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> ```bash
> python test/inductor/test_select_algorithm.py -k test_automatic_cudagraph_policy_takes_precedence_over_profiler
> python test/inductor/test_benchmarking.py -k cudagraph
> lintrunner -a
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> Tests also cover serialized policy, cache identity, GPU discovery from input/output metadata, replay normalization, gradients, thread-local recursion protection, rotating buffers, extern/template routing, and late CUTLASS stream lookup.
>
> ## Checklist
>
> - [x] Passes lint
> - [x] Added or updated tests
> - [x] Updated documentation where applicable
> - [x] Performance claims are limited to measurement correctness
>
> ## BC-breaking?
>
> No.
>
> PR prepared with assistance from an AI tool.

title: [ROCm] Remove -amdgpu-early-inline-all / -amdgpu-function-calls from CK SDPA build and Inductor CK builds
body:
**Summary:**
Removes the `-mllvm -amdgpu-early-inline-all=true` and `-mllvm -amdgpu-function-calls=false` flags from the two places that build Composable Kernel (CK) code on ROCm:
- `aten/src/ATen/CMakeLists.txt` — the `ck_sdpa` static library (`CK_SDPA_EXTRA_HIPCC_FLAGS`), built when `USE_ROCM_CK_SDPA` is on.
- `torch/_inductor/codegen/rocm/compile_command.py` — the Inductor ROCm CK runtime compile options (`_rocm_compiler_options`).

**Motivation:**
`-amdgpu-early-inline-all=true` and `-amdgpu-function-calls=false` force the AMDGPU llvm backend to inline everything.
With the module-wide `AlwaysInliner` now running early in the pipeline, this causes IR growth on the templated CK FMHA kernels, so the `ck_sdpa` build blows up in time/memory. These are compiler-internal debug flags ([llvm/llvm-project#86332](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/86332)) and not tuning knobs. 
In ROCm CK library as well, these options are being phased out. See https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/pull/11183

python test/test_transformers.py -k "ck" -v
- Inductor CK GEMM autotune (ROCm < 7.14 so tests don't skip):

title: [dynamo] Reject non-None returns from traced __init__
body:
I reproduced this myself with a small script. A class whose `__init__` returns a value, for example `return 10`, raises `TypeError: __init__() should return None, not 'int'` in plain Python. With the old build, constructing it inside a compiled function succeeded without any error. That is a wrong result of the kind that makes the real error very hard to see. title: [decomp] Decouple _addmm_activation GELU path from hard-coded CUDA
body:
##Summary

  Decouple _addmm_activation's GELU branch from a hard-coded CUDA check, so that registered third-party backends (via privateuse1, e.g. Ascend NPU) take the
  same fused-tanh GELU fast path as CUDA.

  Changes

  In torch/_decomp/decompositions.py, replace the device logic in _addmm_activation:

  Before:
  if use_gelu:
      if self.is_cuda:
          return aten.gelu(out, approximate="tanh")
      else:
          return aten.gelu(out)

  After:
  if use_gelu:
      private_backend = torch._C._get_privateuse1_backend_name()
      is_accelerator = self.is_cuda or self.device.type == private_backend
      if is_accelerator:
          return aten.gelu(out, approximate="tanh")
      else:
          return aten.gelu(out)

  - Use the public privateuse1 registration interface (torch._C._get_privateuse1_backend_name()) instead of hard-coding CUDA as the only accelerated device.
  - CUDA behavior is unchanged (self.is_cuda still routes to the tanh fast path).
  - Registered privateuse1 backends (e.g. Ascend NPU, "npu") now also take the tanh fast path, matching eager and CUDA behavior.
  - CPU keeps the exact (erf-based) GELU path.
  - This is additive: no existing CUDA path is modified.

##Motivation

  On a privateuse1 backend (e.g. Ascend NPU), is_cuda is False, so the decomposition previously fell into the else branch and computed the exact (erf-based)
  GELU. However, the eager kernel on such backends commonly uses the tanh approximation (as CUDA does). As a result, torch.compile output diverged from eager
  output on the same device, which is problematic for model deployment and validation.

  Aligning third-party backends with the CUDA fast path ensures torch.compile and eager produce consistent results, and avoids unnecessary compute in the
  decomposition path.

  This change follows the general principle of using PyTorch's registered backend mechanism instead of enumerating device names.

##Test Plan

  Verified on real hardware (8x Ascend 910B2, CANN 9.2.0-beta.2, torch_npu 2.15.0.dev):

  - 13/13 unit tests pass:
    - _get_privateuse1_backend_name() returns "npu" for an Ascend-registered environment.
    - NPU tensors route to the tanh fast path (is_accelerator is true).
    - Decomposition output matches aten.gelu(approximate="tanh").
    - torch.compile output matches eager output (max diff 0.0) — the core goal.
    - CPU still uses exact GELU (regression, max diff 0.0).
    - use_gelu=False still routes to ReLU (regression).
  - A CUDA regression test (test_gpu_regression.py) verifies CUDA behavior is unchanged.

##Notes

  - This is a decomposition-path change only; it does not affect eager kernels.
  - torch._C._get_privateuse1_backend_name() returns the default placeholder "privateuseone" when no third-party backend is registered, so behavior on CPU is
    untouched.
  - If a future backend should NOT use the tanh approximation, this can be revisited per-backend; the change here aligns with the common fused-kernel behavior
    shared by CUDA and NPU.

title: [MPS] Check that 1D/2D/3D dispatch grid dims fit in uint32
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198593
* __->__ #198592

`thread_position_in_grid` can only be a 32-bit (or 16-bit) value per axis; the Metal compiler rejects `ulong` for that attribute. `dispatchThreads:` silently truncates the grid width to its low 32 bits

Add a `TORCH_CHECK` in `mtl_dispatch1DJob` and per-axis ones in `mtl_dispatch2DJob` and `mtl_dispatch3DJob`, so any caller exceeding the limit raises instead of producing silently wrong results. Callers that need more threads must split the work (chunks with a base offset, a multi-dimensional grid, or a grid-stride loop).

title: [dynamo] Support backend TensorDescriptor factories
body:
Dynamo previously recognized only the generic Triton TensorDescriptor.from_tensor factory by function identity. Backend subclasses that override or inherit this factory could be rejected in full-graph mode or reconstructed as the generic descriptor class.
    
Capture the concrete descriptor class from class attribute access and require it to round-trip through an importable module and class name. Carry that identity through stable TMA metadata and Inductor IR so TTIR generation, runtime launch, and generated Python wrappers reconstruct the originating factory.
    
Route descriptor imports to the Python JIT and compile-time autotune buffers without emitting Python into generated C++. The AOTI GPU C++ wrapper can construct only the generic CUDA stable descriptor, so reject backend-specific descriptor identities explicitly instead of silently treating them as generic. CPU C++ wrappers cannot construct TMA descriptors, so reject them instead of emitting Python factory calls into generated C++.
    
Add coverage for inherited classmethod factories, import-path validation, the Triton CPU descriptor, Inductor end-to-end codegen, AOTI import routing, and CPU and GPU C++ wrapper rejection.

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Restrict scaled-MM filtering to gfx950
body:
## Summary

The scaled-MM heuristic removes configurations with `BLOCK_K <= 64` when
`get_device_capability() >= (9, 5)`. This restriction targets gfx950, but ROCm
capability tuples contain the `gfx` major and minor rather than an ordered
feature level. The predicate also matches gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200. The normal scaled-MM
path is confirmed reachable on gfx1200, where valid configurations are removed;
the gfx1100 and gfx1151 checks exercise the heuristic directly.

Move the restriction into the ROCm scaled-MM heuristic and match `gfx950`
directly with `rocm_gfx_arch()`. Other ROCm architectures retain their
`BLOCK_K=32` and `BLOCK_K=64` configurations. Other backends are unchanged.

## Validation

`test_scaled_mm_block_k_pruning_is_limited_to_gfx950` is a table-driven
regression test. It patches the reported ROCm architecture and checks the
filtered `BLOCK_K` values:

| Architecture | Expected `BLOCK_K` values |
| --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx1151 | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx1200 | `[32, 64, 128]` |
| gfx950 | `[128]` |

On current main, the three RDNA subcases fail because 32 and 64 are pruned;
the gfx950 case passes. All four cases pass after the change. The test runs
without requiring ROCm hardware.

Separate real-device probes confirmed the before/after behavior:

| Device | Current main | With this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `[128]` | `[32, 64, 128]` |

title: [ROCm] Clamp nearest2d backward launch grid
body:
## Summary

The contiguous `upsample_nearest2d_backward` path derives its launch grid from
`grad_input.numel() / nbatch`. Large inputs can make
`gridDim.x * blockDim.x` exceed HIP's `UINT32_MAX` x-dimension work-size limit,
causing the launch to fail with `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration`.

Clamp the launch grid to the device limit and HIP's work-size limit. When the
full grid cannot be launched, the kernel uses a grid-stride loop to cover the
remaining output. A compile-time flag preserves the existing one-element-per-
thread path for normal-sized inputs.

The batch offset is applied at the output store so the grid-stride cursor is
not modified inside the batch loop. This completes the backward-path TODO from
#180310.

## Validation

`test_upsamplingNearest2d_backward_hip_grid_limit` is the reproducer and
regression guard. It calls the backward operator directly with a
`(1, 1, 65536, 65536)` FP16 input shape, reaching the `2^32` launch boundary
while keeping `grad_output` small.

| Device | Current main | With this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration` | passes |
| gfx1151 | `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration` | passes |
| gfx1200 | `hipErrorInvalidConfiguration` | passes |

The test checks the output shape, total gradient and individual positions, so
it verifies grid-stride indexing rather than only checking that the launch
succeeds.

title: [ROCm] Return power_draw in milliwatts
body:
## Summary

`torch.cuda.power_draw()` returns milliwatts on NVIDIA, where it forwards
`nvmlDeviceGetPowerUsage()`, and watts on ROCm, where it forwards the AMD SMI
socket power reading unchanged. The docstring documents milliwatts, so the ROCm
result is 1000x too small.

Documenting the difference instead is not an option: it is one public function
and a caller cannot branch on the backend to learn the unit. So the ROCm path
converts, and both backends now agree with the documented unit.

The conversion covers both AMD SMI readings, the average socket power and the
current-power fallback used when the average is unavailable. The path where
neither is available is untouched and still returns 0, and no caller
compensated for the watts value, so nothing else in tree changes.

## Validation

`power_draw()` against the AMD SMI reading taken at the same moment:

| Device | AMD SMI | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gfx1100 | 54 W | 54 | 54000 mW |
| gfx1151 | 29 W | 29 | 29000 mW |
| gfx1200 | 14 W | 14 | 14000 mW |

Each row is a pair read back to back, and five consecutive samples per device
gave exactly 1000x.

`test_power_draw` only asserts a non-negative result, which passes either way,
so a new test mocks AMD SMI to pin the unit: average power available, average
unavailable with the current-power fallback, and neither available. Passes on
all three devices.

MI hardware is out of my scope, so please run ROCm CI for MI coverage.

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Keep NVIDIA communication model off HIP
body:
## Summary

`comm_analysis.py` contains an analytical model calibrated for NVIDIA GPU
generations, NCCL protocols and NVLink/InfiniBand topologies. On ROCm it
interprets HIP capability numbers as NVIDIA compute capabilities and treats
peer accessibility as evidence of NVLink.

On two gfx1200 GPUs this selects `BLACKWELL` and `NVLINK_B200`, with an
intra-node bandwidth of 720 GB/s. The measured PCIe peer-to-peer bandwidth is
approximately 54.5 GB/s.

HIP devices no longer enter this NVIDIA model. Their NVIDIA GPU type is
unavailable, their interconnect is reported as unknown, and analytical
bandwidth, runtime and saturation estimates return zero. The existing
backend-native RCCL estimator is unchanged and remains available where the
process group supports it.

Zero means that no calibrated analytical estimate is available. It does not
affect collective execution, but heuristic scheduling may be conservative when
the RCCL estimator is unavailable. This change does not attempt to model PCIe
or xGMI bandwidth.

## Validation

Current-main reproducer on two gfx1200 GPUs:

| GPU type | NVLink | Interconnect | Modelled bandwidth | Measured P2P |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `BLACKWELL` | `True` | `NVLINK_B200` | 720 GB/s | ~54.5 GB/s |

Patched result:

| Device | GPU type | Interconnect | Analytical bandwidth | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| gfx1100 | unavailable | `UNKNOWN` | 0 | pass |
| gfx1151 | unavailable | `UNKNOWN` | 0 | pass |
| gfx1200 | unavailable | `UNKNOWN` | 0 | pass |

A new synthetic regression test patches `torch.version.hip` and verifies that
HIP returns no NVIDIA GPU type, reports no NVLink, selects `UNKNOWN`
interconnect and returns no analytical bandwidth estimate. It fails on current
main and passes with this change.

The existing analytical-fallback and saturation tests were updated for the
neutral ROCm result and pass. The native RCCL estimator was also verified on
two gfx1200 GPUs and returned a nonzero estimate.

Validation is limited to RDNA hardware.

title: Fix autograd.grad graph breaks under aot_eager
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185829

When Dynamo graph-breaks at an unsupported `torch.autograd.grad` call, it normally compiles the prefix and resumes the call in eager mode. AOTAutograd represents differentiably related prefix outputs as sibling outputs, so their edge is not preserved. A valid gradient can become `None`, and a following non-scalar grad call can then behave as if `grad_outputs` was omitted.

This change detects differentiable current-graph targets and values that remain live across the grad break. The liveness walk covers current and inlined parent frames, cells, modified side effects and globals, active exception and context-manager state, backward state, tensor hooks, `save_for_backward` records, dict/set keys, and created or suspended local generators. Unsafe calls skip only the current frame invocation, including through inlining and user context managers; later safe invocations can still compile.

The scope is intentionally `torch.autograd.grad`. Extending the heuristic to `Tensor.backward` or functional backward is unsound without proving terminal use, while an unconditional live-value scan caused normal training, checkpoint lifetime, FlexAttention, and structured-trace regressions. Relationships already severed by an earlier unrelated graph break are a pre-existing limitation outside this change.

Invocation-scoped fallback intentionally retraces repeatedly unsafe calls. A local `torch.utils.benchmark` measurement was 6.81 ms/call versus 40.6 us/call for eager execution. A code-object-wide cached skip was rejected because one unsafe branch would permanently disable compilation for later safe branches.

Fixes #145899

title: mps: expose existing prefill Metal kernel as SDPBackend::flash_attention
body:
## Summary

PyTorch's MPS backend already ships a fused FlashAttention-style prefill Metal kernel (`sdpa_prefill_mps`, #113359). It handles the long-sequence attention path for head\_dims in `{32, 64, 72, 80, 96, 128, 256}` with tiled SIMD threadgroups — **the kernel already exists**. The problem: it was only reachable through `SDPBackend::math`. The `SDPBackend::flash_attention` case had no MPS branch and `_fused_sdp_choice` had no MPS registration, so requesting the flash backend on MPS silently fell through to the CPU path.

This PR wires the existing kernel through the flash-attention dispatch path — **no new Metal code, pure plumbing**.

## Changes

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `aten/src/ATen/native/native_functions.yaml` | Add `MPS: _fused_sdp_choice_mps` to `_fused_sdp_choice`; add `_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_mps` op (mirrors `_for_cpu` signature) |
| `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/Attention.mm` | `_fused_sdp_choice_mps`: returns `flash_attention` when prefill can run (qL > 8, supported head_dim, float/half/bf16, no dropout, no nested tensors); `_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_mps`: thin validated wrapper around existing `sdpa_prefill_mps` |
| `aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/attention.cpp` | Add MPS arm in `SDPBackend::flash_attention` case |
| `torch/_meta_registrations.py` | Meta shape function for new op |
| `test_mps_flash_sdpa.py` | Tests: backend selection, fp32/fp16/bf16 correctness, causal, GQA, error paths |

## Why this matters

Before this PR, on MPS:
```python
with torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION):
    out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
# ↑ silently routed to CPU — wrong device, wrong kernel
```

After this PR, the same code correctly routes through `sdpa_prefill_mps`, the fused Metal kernel. Verified on:
- **Apple M3 8 GB** with ESMC-300M (`head_dim=64`) and ESMC-600M (`head_dim=72`)
- All dtypes: float32, float16, bfloat16
- Causal and non-causal, with and without attention mask, GQA

## Capability gates

`_fused_sdp_choice_mps` returns `math` (falling back to the existing path which internally selects the best available kernel) when any of these hold:
- `PYTORCH_MPS_DISABLE_PREFILL_ATTENTION=1` (existing debug kill-switch)
- Nested tensors
- `dropout_p != 0`
- `head_dim` not in `{32, 64, 72, 80, 96, 128, 256}`
- dtype not in `{float32, float16, bfloat16}`
- `qL <= 8` (vector decode kernel is better for short Q)
- q\_heads not divisible by k\_heads
- mask dtype incompatible (not bool and not matching query dtype)

## Testing

```bash
# On Apple Silicon Mac:
python test_mps_flash_sdpa.py -v
```

All 10 tests pass. The test covers: backend selection for supported/unsupported shapes, output correctness vs math ref (rtol=1e-3), causal masking, GQA, and error paths for dropout/unsupported-head-dim/short-sequence.

## Related

- #113359 — original `sdpa_prefill_mps` kernel
- [Dmitrii Elagин's MPS PR](https://github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm/pull/409) — triggered this investigation: ESMC-600M has `head_dim=72`, which is in the supported set but was never accessible as `flash_attention`

title: [inductor] Codegen backed SymInt input runtime asserts
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185588

When prefer_deferred_runtime_asserts_over_guards=True, Dynamo records backed-SymInt shape checks as deferred runtime asserts instead of guards. FX materializes those backed-only checks as input-graph aten._assert_scalar nodes, but regular Inductor lowering dropped those nodes. Only the AOTI full-runtime-assert path converted input-graph _assert_scalar nodes into wrapper AssertScalar operations, and the unbacked-symbol deferred assert path had no binding point for backed-only expressions.

This teaches Inductor to codegen input-graph _assert_scalar nodes when the assertion expression has backed free symbols and no unbacked symbols. Assertions with unbacked symbols continue to use the existing deferred path so they are emitted only after their unbacked inputs are bound. The fix preserves the existing AOTI full-runtime-assert behavior while covering the regular torch.compile path from the issue.

The alternative was to reject prefer_deferred_runtime_asserts_over_guards under torch.compile, but that would leave the underlying assert codegen gap in place. Emitting the missing wrapper assert fixes the root cause and keeps the config usable.

title: Guard release_available_cached_blocks during CUDA graph capture
body:
Fixes #159594.

## Summary

Guard `release_available_cached_blocks` during CUDA graph capture, matching the existing `release_cached_blocks` retry path.

`release_available_cached_blocks` can release cached blocks through `release_block`, which may call `cudaFree`. Calling `cudaFree` during CUDA graph capture is unsafe and can invalidate the capture.

The broader `release_cached_blocks` retry path already skips cached-block release during actual graph capture via `is_capture_context()`. This applies the same guard to the selective cached-block release path.

The guard only affects real captures, so user mempools (`use_mem_pool` / NCCL / warmup) are unaffected. This path only runs on the OOM retry path.

## Behavior

Before this change, a capture-time allocation failure could enter the selective cached-block release retry path and fail with `cudaErrorStreamCaptureInvalidated`.

After this change, the same case skips cached-block release during capture and reports a clean `OutOfMemoryError` instead.

## Validation

* Reproduced the issue on sm89 and sm120.
* Verified the fix on sm89:

  * before: `AcceleratorError` / `cudaErrorStreamCaptureInvalidated`
  * after: clean `OutOfMemoryError`
* Added a regression test covering the capture-time OOM retry path.

title: Delay RNN graph break until module call
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186614

Dynamo intentionally graph breaks on nn.RNN, nn.GRU, and nn.LSTM when
allow_rnn is disabled. The old implementation raised the unsupported error
while wrapping the recurrent module attribute. For LOAD_ATTR/LOAD_METHOD
bytecode this goes through the generic step graph-break path, which can
compile the prefix but cannot build a continuation for the call site, so the
rest of the frame runs eagerly and post-RNN code is never compiled.

Return a DelayGraphBreakVariable for unsupported recurrent modules instead.
This keeps the attribute load traceable enough to reach the CALL instruction,
where Dynamo's regular call graph-break handling can run the recurrent module
eagerly and resume tracing the continuation. This matches the existing delayed
break pattern used for disabled optimized modules and avoids changing the
experimental allow_rnn=True behavior.

Add regression coverage for RNN, GRU, and LSTM modules that verifies Dynamo
compiles both the pre-recurrent and post-recurrent regions.

> ## Root cause
>
> Mix-order reduction performs each split's partial reduction across the X dimension after running the fused pointwise body. Although masked loads use a fill value, pointwise operations can transform that value into something other than the reduction identity. The partial reduction previously consumed those transformed values without applying `xmask` again, so padded rows could contribute to the result.
>
> ## Fix
>
> For nonconstant X masks, apply `xmask` immediately before each partial X-axis reduction and replace inactive lanes with the identity returned by `ir.Reduction.default_accumulator`. The same identity initializes the accumulator and neutralizes inactive lanes for each reduction type. A singleton logical X extent with mask optimization enabled and a non-fixed X block retains a dynamic mask because the selected `XBLOCK` can exceed one. With mask optimization enabled, a fixed `XBLOCK=1` remains mask-free.
>
> ## Architecture
>
> Applicability: Applicable
>
> Description: The change is localized to mix-order mask selection and the mix-order branch of `TritonKernel.codegen_body`. It enforces the invariant that every value entering a partial X-axis reduction is either produced by a valid X lane or replaced by that reduction's identity. A mask is omitted only when the chosen X block is proven to contain no padded lanes.
>
> Examples: A fused expression such as `x * 2 + 0.25` can turn a masked-load zero into `0.25`. The generated kernel changes inactive lanes back to `0` before a sum or to `1` before a product. A singleton logical X extent still uses `xmask` for a non-fixed X block, while an explicitly fixed `XBLOCK=1` can omit it when mask optimization is enabled.
>
> ## Example
>
> ```python
> import torch
>
>
> def f(x):
>     y = x * 2 + 0.25
>     return y.max(dim=-1).values, y.float().sum(dim=0)
>
>
> x = torch.zeros((40961, 129), dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
> expected = f(x)
> actual = torch.compile(f)(x)
> torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected)
> ```
>
> Before this fix, padded X lanes could contribute transformed values to the column sum; afterward, the compiled result matches eager execution. The row-wise `max` and column-wise `sum` create opposing reduction orders that make the graph eligible for mix-order reduction, but this standalone example does not force or verify that kernel choice. The focused numerical test sets the relevant Inductor configuration and asserts `metrics.codegen_mix_order_reduction == 1`.
>
> ## Testing
>
> The CPU-only code-generation regression passed all four combinations of sum or product with a nonsingleton or singleton X extent:
>

> CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' PYTHONPATH="$PWD${PYTHONPATH:+:$PYTHONPATH}" PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python test/inductor/test_codegen_triton.py -k test_mix_order_partial_accumulate_masks_x -v
> ```

title: Fix export move_to_device_pass device rewrites
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185105

`move_to_device_pass` rewrites device-bearing FX nodes and tensor metadata, but it did not recompile the affected GraphModules. Generated Python could therefore retain stale `_assert_tensor_metadata` device arguments and fail when the moved graph ran directly through `ep.graph_module`.

Recompile every GraphModule touched by the pass so its callable code matches the rewritten graph. Export also supports interpreter-only graphs whose in-memory custom objects cannot be emitted as Python, so keep that existing fallback by ignoring only the same `SyntaxError` raised during code generation.

An earlier version tried to preserve parameter identity with `.data`. Freshly exported state aliases the source module, so that moved source parameters while replacing buffers and left the source module mixed-device. It also corrupted traceable wrapper subclasses by moving only the outer TensorImpl. Retain the existing out-of-place state movement instead, with regressions covering source-module reuse and wrapper-subclass children.

I considered overriding `GraphModule.to()` so it rewrites graph IR, but exported graphs are device-specific and `move_to_device_pass` is the supported graph-casting path. Keeping the fix in that pass avoids changing general FX `GraphModule.to()` semantics.
